[15522] Deploy for real · four agents, one per quadrant

## Correspondence triage, mandate to operation [15523]

[15524] Every artefact filled in, including the ones that are uncomfortable. Very high volume, moderate criticality — the case most departments would call easy. Named honestly it lands in Tier 3 · Enhanced , and that is the most useful thing in this chapter.

[15527] These four agents are composites, not case studies. The figures are internally consistent and illustrative, and the decisions are the ones the sources support. Your organisation will ratify and adapt every one of them.

## Mandate [15531]

## 1 of 10 [15533]

[15534] Signed by the service owner before any build. One page, and it fits.

## Problem [15537]

[15539] Inbound correspondence arrives across six channels into one queue. Median time to first correct routing is four days; 11% is routed wrong at least once. Statutory deadlines are met by escalation, not by process.

## In scope [15542]

[15544] Classify inbound correspondence to one of 34 work queues, extract sender, reference, subject and any stated deadline, and draft a suggested reply from the approved template set.

## Explicitly out of scope [15547]

[15549] Deciding any case. Sending anything. Replying to anyone. Handling correspondence flagged as a complaint, a legal threat, a safeguarding concern or a data-subject request — those route to a human unopened by the agent.

## Success measures [15552]

[15554] Time to correct routing, misroute rate, deadline breaches, and reviewer challenge rate. Not volume processed, and not staff satisfaction alone.

## Decision rights [15557]

[15559] The agent proposes. A caseworker commits. Nothing leaves the organisation without a named person attached to it.

## Funding and duration [15562]

[15564] Twelve months, one delivery team, with a stop point at month four and a re-authorisation decision at month twelve.

## What would make us stop [15567]

[15569] Any statutory deadline missed because of the agent, or a challenge rate below 5% sustained for two months.

## What changes the answer inside this quadrant [15571]

[15572] Same agent, same quadrant, one factor different. Each variant below is scored by the generator on this page, not asserted — so what moves and what does not is the tool's own arithmetic.

[15574] The agent sends the reply itself Tier moves

[15577] + Irreversible Tier 4 · Critical Q1 · Automate with sampling L1 · Draft only — a person edits and commits every output

[15582] One word in the mandate — send rather than draft — and an effect exists that no later correction undoes. Autonomy is forced to draft-only regardless of tier, and shadow mode becomes mandatory. This is the most common scope change requested after go-live, and the cheapest one to refuse.

[15584] Correspondence routinely contains health detail Tier moves

[15587] + Special-category data Tier 4 · Critical Q1 · Automate with sampling L1 · Draft only — a person edits and commits every output

[15592] The screening guardrail stops being a nicety and becomes the control the DPIA rests on. A leakage probe joins the evaluation set, and the grounding index has to be provably free of the material.

[15594] Internal-only queue, rule-based routing Tier moves

## − Discretionary judgement [15599]

## − Vulnerable users [15601]

## Tier 2 · Standard [15603]

## Q1 · Automate with sampling [15605]

## L3 · Act within guardrails — every action logged and sampled [15607]

[15608] Remove the discretion and the vulnerable recipient and the same agent, at the same volume, drops a tier. Most of the governance in the worked example is paid for by those two factors, not by the volume.

[15621] Deploy for real · scope boundary

## What this guide does not cover [15622]

[15623] A guide that does not state its boundary strands the team at the point where the interesting problems start. This chapter exists so nobody reaches gate 3 believing the architecture, the security testing or the legal advice was somewhere in the earlier parts.

## Fully covered here [15626]

[15627] Principles, criticality and tiering, autonomy boundaries, registers and transparency records, oversight design including currency, cost and value modelling, roles and adoption, the pilot method.

## Structured, needs your content [15629]

[15630] Instruction blocks, evaluation plans, threat profiles, DPIA routes, contract clause sets, job redesign. The shape is here; the substance is yours.

## Named but not solved [15632]

[15633] Reference architecture for your estate, engineering pipeline, executed security testing, model selection, sector regulation, organisational design, safety cases.

## What a team must bring [15634]

[15635] Eight things this guide names but cannot supply. Each one has a normal home in an organisation. Find the home before the build starts, not after.

[15637] A target architecture for your estate Enterprise architecture

[15640] This guide names what an architecture must satisfy. It does not know your identity provider, your network, your data platform or your existing contracts. Someone with authority over those has to draw it.

[15642] Executed security testing Security function or an appointed third party

[15645] The threat model here tells you what to test. Running the test — penetration testing, red-teaming, adversarial evaluation — is specialist work with a report at the end of it.

[15647] Legal advice on your specific case Legal and your DPO

[15650] Everything here about lawful basis, automated decision-making and liability is structure for a conversation with a lawyer. It is not the advice.

[15652] Model selection and benchmarking Technical owner

[15655] Which model, at what cost, with what evaluation on your data. This guide is deliberately model-agnostic, which means it cannot answer the question you will be asked first.

[15657] Sector regulation Your regulator and legal

[15660] Health, policing, immigration, education and financial services each carry duties this guide does not enumerate. Where it conflicts with your regulator, your regulator wins.

[15662] Organisational design Accountable leadership

[15665] Who reports to whom, which team holds the capability, and how it is funded past the pilot. The roles here are role names; you have people, budgets and politics.

[15667] Accessibility conformance Accessibility specialist

[15670] The comprehension and inclusion tests here are necessary and not sufficient. A conformance audit against WCAG is a separate, evidenced exercise.

[15672] Safety cases Clinical or safety governance

[15675] Where an agent touches physical safety or clinical outcomes, a structured safety case is required and this guide does not contain one.

## Five things to be honest about [15677]

[15678] Read these before citing anything in this guide to a board, an auditor or a regulator.

## Every artefact here is a proposal [15679]

[15680] Nothing in this guide has statutory force. Until your organisation ratifies it, an artefact is a well-argued suggestion. Ratify it, or expect it to be ignored at the first disagreement.

## Figures marked illustrative are illustrative [15681]

[15682] Where this guide shows a threshold, a percentage or a band, it is a defensible starting point drawn from the sources, not a measured value from your service. Replace it with yours.

## Volume and criticality placements are judgements [15683]

[15684] The fifty-four services in the atlas are placed on published volume bands and an assessment of consequence. They are a starting position for an argument, not a classification you can cite.

## The generator does not approve anything [15685]

[15686] It derives a consistent governance set from the inputs you give it. Give it flattering inputs and it will produce a flattering answer. That is a property of every assessment tool, including the ones with logos on.

## The four worked examples are composites [15687]

[15688] They are built from the sources, from published service data and from patterns that recur across deployments. They are not case studies of four real agents, and no organisation in them is identifiable. Their numbers are internally consistent and illustrative — treat them as a model answer to compare your own against, not as evidence of what happened somewhere.

## Sequence is not schedule [15689]

[15690] The life cycle here is ordered. It carries no durations, because the honest answer depends on your assurance capacity, and that is the constraint nobody plans for.

## Generative, agentic and declarative [3679]

[3680] Three ways of using the same underlying models, with different failure modes and therefore different controls. Most real deployments combine all three, which is exactly why the class needs naming before the controls are chosen.

## Generative [3683]

[3684] Produces content, analysis or options on request. Nothing changes until a person acts on the output.

[3685] You specify: A prompt, grounding sources and an output format.

[3687] Drafting, summarising, translating Analysis and option generation Search and question answering Code and test generation

[3694] Primary failure Plausible but wrong output accepted without review. Tier tendency Usually low to moderate: consequence sits with the person who acts on the output.

[3698] Controls that carry the weight

[3700] Accuracy and grounding evaluation

[3701] Citation and provenance

[3702] Disclosure that AI was used

[3703] Human review before use

## Agentic [3705]

[3706] Takes actions across tools and systems under delegated authority, deciding its own path to a goal.

[3707] You specify: A goal, tools, permissions, guardrails and approval thresholds.

[3709] Triage and routing Multi-step workflow execution System updates within limits Orchestration across services

[3716] Primary failure Correct-looking action taken outside intended scope, or an irreversible action taken without approval. Tier tendency Moderate to high: the agent itself changes the world, so authority and reversibility dominate.

[3720] Controls that carry the weight

[3722] Capability separated from authority

[3723] Least-privilege permissions and recertification

[3724] Approval gates for consequential actions

[3725] Full action logging and rollback

## Declarative [3727]

[3728] You state the outcome, rules and boundaries; the platform resolves how they are met and keeps behaviour inside the declaration.

[3729] You specify: Instructions, knowledge sources, permitted actions and constraints — as configuration, not code.

[3731] Configured assistants defined by a manifest Policy and rules expressed as configuration Low-code flows with declared triggers Templated agents published to a team

[3738] Primary failure The declaration drifts from intent, or nobody owns the specification that is now running in production. Tier tendency Varies with what is declared: the specification is the control surface, so review it as you would code.

[3742] Controls that carry the weight

[3744] Version control over the declaration

[3745] Named owner for the specification

[3746] Change assessment on every edit

[3747] Regression tests against the declared outcome

[3758] Who chooses the path The person The agent, within guardrails The platform, within the declaration

[4063] MCP server An open-protocol endpoint that exposes tools and resources to any MCP-capable client. Tools can be discovered at runtime, so capability can change without the agent being republished.

[4068] Connector Brings an external system’s content into an AI tool’s index or grounding, such as Copilot connectors.

[4073] Plugin or action A packaged custom action, such as an MCP or API plugin in a declarative agent, that lets an agent read or change data.

[4078] Add-in or app An extension that runs inside a host application, such as an Office add-in or a chat app.

[4083] API and webhook Direct integration through REST APIs, OpenAPI descriptions or event webhooks.

[4088] Integrator or gateway A platform that brokers many connections, applies policy and logs traffic, such as an MCP gateway or integration platform.

## Nine controls for every connector, plugin and MCP server [4186]

[4188] Register every connector, plugin and MCP server in the tool and data-source registers, with a named owner.

[4212] Architecture & quality

## Principles with tests, gates with teeth [4213]

[4214] A three-tier canon governs everything that influences how something is built — prototypes explicitly included, because most principle breaches enter the estate through prototypes that were never intended to survive, and then did.

## Tier 1 — mandated, cited not restated [4216]

[4217] T1-01 Secure by Design T1-02 CAF & GovAssure T1-03 Technology Code of Practice T1-04 GDS Service Standard T1-05 AI Playbook T1-06 Data protection & public records T1-07 WCAG 2.2 AA

[4225] Tier 1 conformance is binary: the principle applies and is met, or a recorded exception exists. No informal partial conformance.

## Tier 2 — the core seven, each with a test [4226]

## AP-01 [4229]

## Federated, not centralised [4231]

[4233] Test: Can each element be traced to a named authoritative owner outside the central platform? Looks compliant, is not: "We will federate later, once everything is in one place."

## AP-02 [4238]

## Discovery separated from access [4240]

[4242] Test: Can a user discover an asset exists without thereby gaining access to it? Looks compliant, is not: Endpoint or credential details published as discovery metadata for convenience.

## AP-03 [4247]

## Human-in-the-loop by design [4249]

[4251] Test: Can any automated component write to the record without recorded human approval? Looks compliant, is not: "The user can always review it" — optional review presented as a control.

## AP-04 [4256]

## Traceability & provenance mandatory [4258]

[4260] Test: Take any output at random: can you reconstruct inputs, owner, decision and evidence without asking a person? Looks compliant, is not: Evidence linked at closure rather than at capture.

## AP-05 [4265]

## Reuse before build [4267]

[4269] Test: Is there a recorded reuse assessment that predates the build decision? Looks compliant, is not: Reuse assessment performed after the build decision, to justify it.

## AP-06 [4274]

## Accessible & inclusive by design [4276]

[4278] Test: Is accessibility evidence produced before release? Does every status carry a non-colour cue? Looks compliant, is not: "We will run an accessibility audit before go-live" as the only accessibility activity.

## AP-07 [4283]

## Guardrails enforced, not documented [4285]

[4287] Test: Attempt to breach the control through the normal interface. Does it succeed? Looks compliant, is not: A mandatory gate with no exception path — guaranteeing informal workarounds.

[4290] Prototype promotion gate. A prototype may not be promoted toward live use until Tier 1 and Tier 2 conformance is assessed and recorded. Record intended lifespan and disposal point at creation; record deferred principles; re-assess them at the gate. Human-in-the-loop applies in full even at prototype stage — autonomy introduced early is rarely removed later. Promotion is a decision, not a drift.

## The assurance-gated agentic pattern [4293]

[4294] From the AI Engineering Lab's reference implementation: the transferable innovation is not any one use case — it is the operating model around it. Specialist agents routed by an orchestrator; a challenger agent that reviews outputs; a compliance agent; assurance gates executed in the workflow; immutable audit trails; human approval before anything writes to the record. The same pattern serves capability management, catalogue operations, workforce planning and architecture governance.

[4295] Specialist agents Orchestrator routing Challenger agent Compliance agent Assurance gates in-workflow Immutable audit trail Human approval to write Escalation paths

## The quality gate — score prototypes like you mean it [4304]

[4305] A gate, not a form: run at the end of every iteration. Tier 0 is the brake — the only tier that can argue for less; a veto is the instrument doing its job. Scores are capped by evidence strength, unscoreable items go on an open register published with the score, and demo drift — a level-3 prototype someone useful quietly relies on — is the most common governance failure in this class of work.

## Where should the information live? [4689]

[4690] Work down the questions in order. The first "yes" is your answer — the goal is the right information, to the right people, at the right time, securely and efficiently.

## 1. Is the information already in an authoritative source (for example an existing SharePoint site, policy library, DMS)? [4693]

[4695] Yes → Use existing authoritative location — keep content in place, ensure agent uses existing permissions, maintain single source of truth, lower duplication and maintenance risk.

## 2. Can the agent be granted access via existing permissions? [4699]

[4701] Yes → Grant access via existing permissions — respect least privilege, use groups and roles already in place, review access periodically.

## 3. Can permissions be adjusted for a new site (or team) without creating excessive oversharing or security risk? [4705]

[4707] Yes → Adjust permissions or create a secure location — create dedicated site or library if needed, configure granular permissions, review with the information owner.

## 4. Is copying or moving content necessary for the agent to function effectively? [4711]

[4713] Yes → Copy or move content with strong controls — risk of duplication and divergence, increased maintenance and update process, maintain links back to source of truth, confirm retention and records handling.

[4719] Use metadata, views, filters or connectors

[4720] Use automated search over authoritative sources

[4722] Avoid unnecessary duplication

[4734] Maintenance — Can the team keep copies current and in sync with the source?

[4736] Licensing & cost — Do users have the right licences? Any connector or storage costs?

[4738] Records & retention — Where is the record of business? How long must it be kept?

## A builder's design choice sets a budget holder's cost [9203]

[9204] AI cost is a portfolio, not a licence line. You are billed per token, in and out — roughly four characters or three-quarters of a word each; an A4 page is 600–800 tokens. Micro-costs stack when an agent runs on repeat. Report by service, product, agent, owner, model and cost driver; showback before chargeback; no expenditure classification without finance-led assessment.

## Microsoft Copilot [9228]

[9229] Cost: a per-user licence ($30 per month list) covers Chat and Copilot in the Office apps. Cowork, Code, Autopilot and frontier models consume Copilot Credits at $0.01 each on pay-as-you-go. Agent security for custom agents needs Agent 365.

[9231] Residency: follows the tenant's Microsoft 365 geography. Web grounding, subprocessor models (Claude, Grok) and Code apps on Managed Runtime need separate checks.

## Anthropic Claude [9234]

[9235] Cost: a seat per user, plus usage at token rates by model (Opus 5.5 lists at $4 input / $20 output per million tokens). Model routing, effort settings and prompt caching are the main levers.

[9237] Residency: set by deployment route. Anthropic-processed with a US-only option, or in-region through Bedrock, Google Cloud or Foundry. Connectors carry the content they fetch to the model.

# Live pilot

[Open this section on the publisher’s website](https://cyberdudeuk.github.io/ai-capability-governance/#part-live-pilot)

The numbers in brackets identify elements in the ordered DOM inventory. This is a text projection of Em’s material.

[12623] Part 8 of 12 · 9 chapters

## Live pilot [12624]

[12633] Live pilot handbook · prototype pilot pack, 25 August 2026

## Testing this guide through a real deployment [12634]

[12635] We are not reviewing a document. We are using the playbook during a live AI deployment to determine whether it improves decisions, delivery, assurance and public-service outcomes, and whether there is sufficient evidence and appetite to establish a permanent, interactive toolkit.

[12638] Evidence status. The pilot model, thresholds and templates are proposed practice. They must be agreed for the selected live deployment. No pilot outcome is claimed in advance.

## Seven stages, seven decisions [12640]

## Mobilise [12644]

[12646] Is the pilot worth initiating?

[12647] Mandate, sponsor, scope and evaluation plan. Proceed or stop.

## Select [12653]

[12655] Is the deployment suitable and safe for a pilot?

[12656] Candidate assessment and baseline. Select, condition or reject.

## Prepare [12662]

[12664] Are people, controls, evidence and fallbacks ready?

[12665] Readiness and assurance plan. Authorise controlled deployment.

## Deploy [12671]

[12673] Can the playbook be used during real delivery?

[12674] Operational evidence and decision trail. Continue, restrict, pause or stop.

## Challenge [12680]

[12682] Did governance and assurance improve decisions?

[12683] Independent findings and participant evidence. Accept, remediate or retest.

## Evaluate [12689]

[12691] Was the playbook useful, proportionate and valuable?

[12692] Evaluation and options appraisal. Stop, retain, simplify or evolve.

## Decide [12698]

[12700] Is there appetite and evidence for a permanent capability?

[12701] Investment recommendation and roadmap. Toolkit decision.

## Sponsor or SRO [12707]

[12742] Live pilot · hypothesis and test dimensions

## What the pilot is testing [12743]

[12744] Primary hypothesis: using the playbook during a live deployment will improve the clarity, consistency, traceability and proportionality of governance and assurance without imposing unjustified delivery burden.

## Usability [12748]

[12750] People can find and apply the right guidance without the author present.

[12752] Task observation, completion, help requests and interviews.

## Proportionality [12755]

[12757] Controls reflect risk, autonomy, data, decision influence and public effect.

[12759] Exceptions, duplicated work, effort diary and reviewer judgement.

## Decision quality [12762]

[12764] Material decisions have clear owners, evidence, uncertainty and conditions.

[12766] Decision records and assurance sampling.

## Delivery value [12769]

[12771] The playbook prevents rework or reveals issues early enough to act.

[12773] Before and after comparison, avoided rework and issue chronology.

[12774] Assurance quality Claims are tested against meaningful evidence. Findings, closure evidence and independent opinion.

[12778] Learning value Participants gain usable capability and confidence. Applied assessments, job-aid use and follow-up interviews.

## Future demand [12784]

[12786] Teams and leaders prefer a maintained toolkit over no framework or a static document.

[12788] Investment survey, sponsor decision and committed use cases.

## Non-objectives [12789]

[12793] Proving that every AI deployment should use identical controls.

[12797] Treating participant satisfaction as proof of safety or value.

[12801] Using a successful pilot to claim cross-government impact.

[12805] Replacing formal legal, security, privacy, commercial or service-assessment obligations.

[12806] Back to the contents · Suggest a correction (opens GitHub)

[12818] Live pilot · candidate selection

## Choosing a deployment worth learning from [12819]

[12820] Seven criteria, the evidence each needs, and the condition that turns a candidate into a rejection or an escalation.

## Real deployment [12823]

[12826] Named service, users, owner and intended live or limited-live use.

[12828] Reject or escalate when: There is only a hypothetical demo.

## Bounded purpose [12830]

[12831] Defined tasks, prohibited uses and measurable outcomes. Reject or escalate when: Purpose is open-ended or unowned.

## Safe test route [12835]

[12838] Controlled environment, data route, fallback and stop mechanism.

[12840] Reject or escalate when: Critical safeguards are unavailable.

## Representative learning [12842]

[12845] The candidate exercises meaningful parts of the playbook.

[12847] Reject or escalate when: The use case is too trivial to generate evidence.

## Team capacity [12849]

[12852] Product, operational, technical and governance participation.

[12854] Reject or escalate when: Delivery relies on one person or unavailable specialists.

## Evidence access [12856]

[12859] Permission to examine decisions, tests, incidents and effort.

[12861] Reject or escalate when: Evaluation cannot access material evidence.

## Change tolerance [12863]

[12866] Team accepts challenge and can alter or pause deployment.

[12868] Reject or escalate when: Go-live is predetermined regardless of evidence.

## Recommended cohort [12870]

[12871] Use three contrasting deployments where feasible: a bounded low-risk assistant, a reusable internal knowledge or workflow agent, and a higher-impact agent influencing operational judgement. This is a suggested design, not a mandated sample.

[12872] Back to the contents · Suggest a correction (opens GitHub)

## Seventeen roles, one accountable line [12885]

[12886] The deployment SRO stays accountable for the live service throughout. The pilot adds evaluation and independent challenge; it does not take accountability away from delivery.

[12896] Pilot SRO Accountable for pilot outcomes, scope and residual risk.

[12926] Tests usability and captures staff and affected-user evidence.

## Service designer [12930]

[12938] Builds bounded capability and supplies evaluation and operational evidence.

## Data and information lead [12942]

## Security and privacy leads [12948]

## Responsible AI and accessibility leads [12954]

[12956] Challenge fairness, human control, inclusion and public impact.

## Learning and change lead [12960]

[12962] Delivers induction, job aids, competence assessment and adoption support.

## Independent assurance lead [12966]

[12968] Plans and conducts evidence-based challenge independent of delivery.

## Evaluation lead [12972]

## Community reviewers [12978]

[12999] Live pilot · formal assurance model

## Five assurance stages, five kinds of opinion [13000]

[13001] Each stage states what it is for, what evidence it reviews, and the opinions it can legitimately reach.

## Readiness [13004]

[13005] Determine whether controlled deployment can begin.

[13008] Evidence: Scope, owners, risk, authority, data, tests, fallback, training.

## Opinion: Ready; ready with conditions; not ready. [13010]

## In-flight [13012]

[13013] Test whether controls operate and the playbook supports decisions.

[13016] Evidence: Logs, samples, incidents, exceptions, user evidence, decisions.

## Opinion: Effective; partially effective; ineffective. [13018]

## Change [13020]

[13021] Assess material changes to model, tools, data, purpose or service.

[13024] Evidence: Impact assessment, regression tests, permissions and updated record.

## Opinion: Authorise; condition; retest; reject. [13026]

## Close-out [13028]

[13029] Judge whether claims and conclusions are supported.

[13032] Evidence: Outcome evidence, costs, findings, limitations and participant testimony.

## Opinion: Reasonable; qualified; insufficient assurance. [13034]

## Investment [13036]

[13037] Assess whether permanence is justified.

[13040] Evidence: Need, repeat demand, value, maintainability, ownership and funding.

## Opinion: Stop; static guide; simplify; interactive toolkit. [13042]

## Independence rule [13044]

[13045] Delivery teams own controls and evidence. Independent assurance challenges claims and reports limitations. The SRO makes the accountable decision; assurance does not transfer accountability.

[13046] Back to the contents · Suggest a correction (opens GitHub)

[13058] Live pilot · journey and rhythm

## End-to-end pilot journey [13059]

[13060] Ten steps from mobilise to share, each with its activities and the artefact it must produce.

## Mobilise [13064]

## Pilot charter, RACI, evaluation protocol, communication calendar. [13066]

## Select [13068]

## Candidate scorecard, selection decision and conditions. [13070]

[13073] Brief all roles; assess learning needs; issue playbook routes and job aids; rehearse escalation.

## Operational evidence, incidents, feedback and change log. [13086]

## Challenge [13088]

## Evaluate [13092]

[13093] Compare baseline; triangulate metrics, observation and interviews; document limitations.

## Decide [13096]

## Decision record, investment recommendation and roadmap. [13098]

## Share [13100]

## Lessons pack and controlled reusable assets. [13102]

## Candidate interview [13107]

[13109] Pilot, deployment and assurance leads.

[13110] Test eligibility, constraints and evidence access. Selection record.

[13121] Align purpose, boundaries, responsibilities and stop routes.

[13132] Review decisions, friction, incidents, metrics and learning.

[13141] Test controls and conditions; decide remedial action. Assurance note and decision.

## Participant pulse [13147]

[13149] Users and delivery team.

[13150] Capture usability and burden close to the work. Short structured feedback.

## Mid-point challenge [13156]

[13158] Independent reviewers and community representatives.

[13159] Identify blind spots before conclusions harden. Challenge findings.

## Close-out review [13165]

[13167] All accountable and assurance roles.

[13168] Agree evidence, limitations and recommendations. Final assurance opinion.

## Investment gate [13174]

[13177] Choose future option. Investment decision.

## Nine moments, one honest message [13193]

[13194] Each moment names its audience, message, channel and owner. The framework is being assessed — not the teams taking part.

## Pre-launch [13199]

## Applicants [13221]

[13223] Decision note and direct conversation. Pilot SRO.

## Participants and sponsors [13241]

[13243] Weekly digest and monthly dashboard. Pilot manager.

## Challenge [13249]

## Assurance and community [13251]

[13252] Focused review question, evidence boundaries and response route.

[13253] Review pack and facilitated session. Assurance lead.

## All participants [13261]

## Investment [13269]

[13273] Decision paper and deck. Pilot SRO.

## Wider sharing [13279]

[13283] Community session and controlled publication. Communications owner.

## Core messages [13286]

[13290] This is a controlled test of the framework in real delivery.

[13294] Participation is not an audit of team performance.

[13319] Live pilot · success framework and feedback

## Twelve measures, no invented thresholds [13320]

[13321] Each measure names its evidence, owner and cadence. Thresholds are agreed after the baseline is captured: a pre-set percentage without context would create false precision.

## Independent use [13324]

[13325] Participants navigate lifecycle and required artefacts without author dependency.

[13326] Observed task completion; help requests; navigation errors. Evaluation lead. Baseline and end.

## Proportionality [13331]

[13332] Teams and reviewers agree controls match material risk and consequence.

[13335] Effort diary; duplicated controls; exceptions; reviewer judgement.

## Assurance lead. [13337]

[13339] Weekly and close-out.

## Decision traceability [13341]

[13342] Material decisions identify owner, evidence, uncertainty, conditions and review.

[13343] Decision-record sample. Pilot manager. Fortnightly.

## Early issue detection [13348]

[13349] Material gaps are discovered while action remains possible.

[13350] Issue chronology and avoided or reduced rework evidence. Service owner. Monthly.

## Assurance quality [13355]

[13356] Findings distinguish intent, design, implementation, operation and outcome.

[13357] Independent assurance quality review. Assurance lead. Mid-point and close.

## Operational readiness [13362]

[13363] Support, monitoring, fallback and incident routes work in exercises and operation.

[13364] Readiness checks, exercises and operational records. Operations lead. Pre-live and live.

## Learning efficacy [13369]

[13370] Participants demonstrate relevant competence in realistic tasks.

[13371] Applied assessment and coaching records. Learning lead. Before and after.

## User and service value [13376]

[13377] Observed service outcomes improve or credible learning justifies continuation.

[13378] Service-specific baseline and evaluation. Product manager. Agreed cadence.

## Burden and cost [13383]

[13384] Implementation effort and recurring cost are visible and acceptable relative to value.

[13385] Time, support and consumption data. Evaluation and finance. Monthly.

## Demand and appetite [13390]

[13391] Leaders and teams prefer a maintained option and commit use cases, ownership or resources.

[13392] Structured option choice and commitments. Toolkit product owner. Close-out.

## Evidence integrity [13397]

[13398] Claims separate verified results, internal evidence, assumptions and expected outcomes.

[13399] Evidence audit. Independent assurance. Close-out.

## Inclusion [13404]

[13405] Research and controls address accessibility and affected-user differences.

[13406] Accessibility and inclusion evidence. Accessibility lead. Design and close-out.

## Feedback as formal evidence [13410]

[13411] Observed use Whether participants can apply the guide in context. At key lifecycle tasks. Observe the framework, not individual performance.

[13416] Decision sampling Whether governance claims are traceable. Throughout deployment. Risk-based sample agreed in advance.

[13421] Effort diary Where burden, duplication and rework occur. Weekly. Record estimates honestly and label them.

[13426] Structured interviews What helped, hindered or remained missing. Baseline, mid-point, close. Separate experience from factual claims.

[13431] Tabletop scenarios Whether controls work under failure and uncertainty. Pre-live and mid-point. Use synthetic scenarios where appropriate.

## Assassin review [13438]

[13440] Where the model could fail, be gamed or become bureaucratic.

[13442] Mid-point.

[13444] Facilitated, blameless challenge.

[13445] Independent evidence review Whether conclusions follow from evidence. Close-out. Declare conflicts and evidence limitations.

[13450] Option-preference survey Whether appetite exists for future forms. Close-out. Require rationale and commitment, not preference alone.

[13455] Community consultation Whether patterns transfer beyond the pilot. After initial evidence. Do not generalise from advocacy alone.

## Feedback taxonomy [13460]

[13463] KEEP

[13464] Works and should remain.

## Protect and evidence. [13465]

[13467] IMPROVE

[13468] Useful but unclear or incomplete.

## Refine and retest. [13469]

[13471] REMOVE

[13472] Adds unjustified burden or duplicates controls.

## Remove or explain exception. [13473]

[13475] MISSING

[13476] A necessary need or control is absent.

## Add, assign owner, validate. [13477]

[13479] CONFLICT

[13480] Contradicts policy, service or assurance practice.

## Escalate and resolve. [13481]

[13483] LOCALISE

[13484] Valid but needs context-specific adaptation.

## Create configurable pattern. [13485]

[13498] Live pilot · decision and future state

## What happens after the pilot [13499]

[13500] Four options, the conditions that select each, and what each commits the organisation to. No option is pre-selected.

## Stop [13504]

[13505] Value is weak, burden is excessive, risks are unresolved or demand is absent.

[13506] Archive evidence and retain lessons; do not operationalise.

## Retain static playbook [13508]

[13509] The guide is useful as reference but repeat operational demand is limited.

[13510] Assign light-touch ownership and scheduled review.

## Simplify and retest [13512]

[13514] Value exists but usability or proportionality is inadequate.

[13515] Prioritise critical changes and conduct focused retest.

## Build living toolkit [13517]

[13518] Evidence shows repeat need, practical value, appetite and sustainable ownership.

[13519] Fund discovery and product development for an ongoing service.

## Investment evidence required for option D [13521]

[13522] Multiple committed user groups or deployments, not general interest alone.

[13523] A named product or service owner and multidisciplinary maintenance capacity.

[13524] A sustainable source of policy, standards and pattern updates.

[13525] Clear content governance, versioning, supersession and retirement rules.

[13526] Evidence that dynamic interaction adds value beyond a downloadable guide.

[13527] Security, privacy, accessibility, information-management and operating-cost assessment.

[13528] A measurable service outcome and roadmap, not only a feature list.

## Future-state toolkit concept [13529]

## Flagship implementation guide [13531]

[13534] Understand the end-to-end route.

[13536] Adaptive journey through lifecycle, roles, gates and evidence.

[13538] Evidence: Navigation, completion and repeat-use data.

## Governance navigator [13540]

[13543] Know which controls and forums apply.

[13545] Context-led route based on purpose, risk, autonomy and public effect.

[13547] Evidence: Routing errors, exceptions and decision consistency.

## Internal ATRS workspace [13549]

[13552] Create and maintain a transparency record.

[13554] Guided record, evidence links, review and publication decision.

[13556] Evidence: Field usability, maintenance burden and scope decisions.

## Assurance workspace [13558]

[13559] Build and review an evidence-based assurance case. Claims, evidence, findings, conditions and closure. Evidence: Evidence quality and review efficiency.

## Learning academy [13564]

[13565] Build competence by responsibility. Role pathways, scenarios, assessment and job aids. Evidence: Competence outcomes and support demand.

## Pattern library [13570]

[13571] Reuse proven controls and artefacts. Versioned patterns with evidence, owner and applicability. Evidence: Verified reuse and reduced duplication.

## Portfolio control tower [13576]

[13577] Oversee value, risk, cost and lifecycle. Inventory, status, evidence freshness and decision queues. Evidence: Decision usefulness and data quality.

## Community feedback loop [13582]

[13585] Keep the toolkit relevant.

[13587] Structured proposals, challenge, supersession and release notes.

[13589] Evidence: Contribution quality and maintenance capacity.

[13591] Product principle: the implementation guide remains the flagship resource. Interactive functions should reduce cognitive load and help people act safely; they must not hide accountability, evidence or applicable authoritative guidance.

## Participant checklist [13592]

## Before deployment [13595]

[13597] Read assigned playbook route.

[13598] Complete induction and competence tasks.

[13599] Confirm purpose, authority and prohibited use.

[13600] Validate data, tools and owners.

[13601] Practise fallback and escalation.

## During deployment [13603]

[13605] Use approved process and boundaries.

[13606] Record material decisions and uncertainty.

[13607] Report incidents and friction promptly.

[13608] Maintain evidence and effort diary.

[13609] Attend evidence clinics and assurance reviews.

## At close-out [13611]

[13613] Complete interview and option survey.

[13614] Review evidence and factual accuracy.

[13615] Declare unresolved concerns.

[13616] Identify KEEP, IMPROVE, REMOVE or MISSING.

[13617] Confirm future interest and commitment.

## Pilot safety stop rules [13619]

[13621] Immediate or plausible material harm to users or the public.

[13622] Loss of control over permissions, data or state-changing actions.

[13623] Critical security, privacy, legal or accessibility condition breached.

[13624] Required human oversight or operational fallback unavailable.

[13625] Evidence integrity compromised in a way that prevents accountable decision-making.

[13626] Deployment moves outside approved purpose or environment.

## Avoiding the “access database moment” [7906]

[7907] How a small, helpful agent becomes business critical without visibility or control. Small agents can create big value — and big risk. Visibility, ownership and governance early in the journey prevent unmanaged tools from becoming unmanageable dependencies.

[7910] 1 Personal experiment Low visibility An individual creates an agent to solve a personal problem or save time.

[7915] 2 Shared with team Low to moderate visibility Shared with colleagues or a small team to help with common tasks.

[7920] 3 Wider adoption Rising visibility More teams discover it and start using it organically.

[7925] 4 Dependence builds Rising to high visibility Critical work starts to rely on the agent and its outputs.

[7930] 5 Business critical High visibility Used across the department or service. Business processes become dependent on it.

[7935] 6 Invisible criticality Gap in visibility No formal ownership, limited documentation, unknown controls, unknown costs.

[7940] 7 High risk exposure Critical · unmanaged Risk of failure, data breach, inaccurate decisions or service disruption.

[7945] 8 Event of failure Loss of trust and value Agent breaks, data changes or owner leaves — causing a real operational impact.

[7956] 2. Require description Purpose & use case · Data sources · Support owner · Review dates

[7959] 3. Assign ownership Business owner · Technical owner · Information owner · Risk owner

[7962] 4. Assess & classify Risk & impact · Data sensitivity · Criticality score · Assurance needs

[7965] 5. Control & assure Approved sources · Guardrails · Human oversight · Testing & validation

[7968] 6. Monitor & review Usage & performance · Cost & consumption · Accuracy & quality · Incident tracking

[7971] 7. Promote or remediate Move to managed platform (e.g. Copilot Studio) · Or retire / remediate

## Accountable, transparent and auditable [8122]

## Applied throughout every stage [8124]

## Capability is not authority [8133]

[8134] An agent may be able to do many things, but can only do what it is authorised to do. Capability is about potential; authority is about permission. Capability + authority + context = action — only when all controls are satisfied can the agent act.

## What the agent can do — capability [8137]

[8138] Technical potential and skills: the full range of capabilities, knowledge, tools and actions the agent is built or enabled to perform.

[8139] Natural language understanding Tool use & API integrations Reasoning & problem solving Workflow orchestration & scheduling Data retrieval (RAG) Analysis & visualisation Code generation & automation Communication (drafting, email, chat) Content creation & summarisation Learning from feedback

## Governance controls [8151]

[8152] Bridging capability to appropriate action.

[8153] Policies & rules Organisational policies, legal requirements and ethical guardrails define boundaries.

[8155] Delegated authority Explicit permissions granted for specific tasks, data and systems.

[8157] Conditions & controls Context, thresholds, approvals and risk checks must be satisfied.

[8159] Human oversight People remain in control of decisions and can intervene or override.

[8161] Monitoring & audit Actions are logged, monitored and reviewed for assurance and compliance.

## What the agent is allowed to do — authority [8164]

[8165] Permitted actions in the right context, within defined boundaries, for specific purposes and users.

[8166] Draft policy briefing Approved for Policy Team (sensitivity: OFFICIAL)

[8168] Send standard email response Approved with template and review

[8170] Summarise documents up to OFFICIAL Approved with data classification filter

[8172] Update internal tracker or system Approved with role-based permissions

[8174] Escalate issue to human reviewer Required when confidence below threshold

## Why separate capability from authority [8177]

[8180] Reduces risk Limits exposure by ensuring agents cannot act beyond intent or policy.

[8183] Improves accountability Clear ownership and delegated authority for all actions.

[8186] Supports compliance Meets legal, regulatory and ethical obligations.

[8189] Enables agility Adjust permissions without rebuilding capabilities.

[8192] Builds trust Transparent controls and oversight build confidence.

[8195] Adapts to context Decisions and permissions can vary by role, risk and situation.

[8435] Human oversight · runbook

## Twelve steps to stand up proportionate oversight [8436]

[8437] A runbook for a service or department starting human oversight of AI, with starting positions for the governance documents it will need. The templates are skeletons, not legal advice: take them to your data protection officer, equality lead and legal adviser. From the Responsible AI and Data Use (RAIDU) work, merged into this playbook on 22 November 2026. Each item keeps its evidence grade: Proposed items are design proposals for review, not policy or established practice.

[8441] Before anything: is this for you? (Adopt) Run the classifier against your two or three largest AI deployments. All assist-class? Tier-1 telemetry and resourced oversight declaration; stop there. Anything determine-class? Work through the whole runbook. Mostly recommend-class? Tiers 1 and 2; read reversibility question carefully.

[8448] Who is needed (Adopt)

[8452] Weeks 1–2 — decide and disclose (Adopt) Classify every AI deployment in the service. Add each to the register. Export it. Brief the SRO on the register summary, particularly anything determine-class that cannot evidence its safeguard works. Open the DPIA and the union conversation in the same week. Both get harder the longer you leave them, and the union one cannot be recovered if it starts late. Write the resourced oversight declaration for the largest deployment.

[8459] Weeks 3–6 — emit tier 1 (Adopt) Map your existing approval telemetry onto the seven tier-1 fields. Most case management systems already hold all seven; the work is naming, not capture. Emit to the standard vocabulary codes. Resist local variants — the point is comparability. Run run_baseline.py or drop the CSV into the instrument. Expect the tier-1 warning that you cannot yet assess decay. That warning is the finding.

[8465] Weeks 7–10 — reach tier 2 (Adopt) Add edit distance, reason capture, streak count and model version. Streak must be derived from the real sequence. A field that disagrees with its own sequence is worse than an absent one. First real reading. Report it to the SRO whatever it says.

[8471] Weeks 11–12 — decide about tier 3 (Adopt) If the service is determine-class, start the ethics and union route for canaries now. It is the long pole. If not, stay at tier 2 and revisit in six months. Publish the baseline internally. Including if it shows nothing — a null result honestly reported is what makes this evidence-led rather than advocacy.

[8477] Integration (Adopt)

[8481] What to expect to go wrong (Adopt) The union conversation started too late. Recoverable only by stopping and restarting. Start it in week 1. Someone asks for individual-level breakdowns. Refuse. It is technically unavailable in the aggregator by design; keep it that way. Once it exists it will be requested by someone senior enough to get it. The first reading looks bad and there is pressure to withhold it. A withheld baseline is worse than no baseline, because you now know and cannot say you did not. Tier-1 data reported as reassurance. It cannot detect decay. The instrument says so explicitly for this reason. Local vocabulary variants. Every unprefixed local code destroys comparability. Use x_ and propose the addition centrally.

[8489] Ninety-day MVP (earlier version) (Superseded sequence) Instrument one live decision-support deployment with the P1 event schema (two weeks of engineering) Add predict-then-reveal on the highest-consequence decision type only Establish unaided baseline from priors captured in first month Publish aggregate result to service owner and Hub — including if it shows nothing Run first canary batch under ethics approval, aggregate only, agreed with unions in advance Write up event schema and prior-capture component as reusable spec

[8498] What departments are asked to do (README) (Programme) Map existing telemetry onto the event schema Add predict-then-reveal on one high-consequence decision type Run run_baseline.py against real events instead of simulated ones Publish the aggregate result, including if it shows nothing

[8505] Immediate sequence post-MoG (Programme) Establish where the AI assurance profession work landed Submit the ministerial brief Contact MHCLG Local AI and the LGA Offer the schema and pipeline to GDS in DCMS as a candidate first delivery artefact Identify one department willing to be instrumented

[8513] Recommended order to publication (Programme) Repository Pilot Exemplar Accessibility conformance Publication

## Governance templates [8521]

## Data protection impact assessment — starting positions [8523]

[8525] Is a DPIA required? Probably yes at tier 2 and certainly at tier 3. The processing concerns staff conduct at work, involves systematic monitoring of a workforce, and relates to the evaluation of performance — even though the design deliberately prevents individual evaluation. Argue it through rather than assuming the aggregation exempts you.

[8526] The question your DPO will ask: if it is genuinely non-identifying, why does it need a DPIA? Answer: because the collection point is identifying, and because the risk being assessed is function creep, not the current design.

## Equality impact assessment — the questions that actually bite [8528]

[8530] The generic template will not surface the real issues. These will.

[8531] Differential effect of friction. Cognitive forcing interventions benefit people with higher need for cognition more than others. Uniform application therefore produces unequal benefit. Who is disadvantaged — staff with dyslexia, ADHD, English as an additional language, high caseloads, caring responsibilities affecting available concentration?

[8532] Reasonable adjustments. Does predict-then-reveal interact badly with any assistive technology in use? Has it been tested with a screen reader, with magnification, and at the time pressure a real queue applies?

[8533] Cohort composition. If cohorts map to teams, and teams differ systematically in composition, aggregate comparison between cohorts can become proxy discrimination. Check before publishing cohort comparisons.

[8534] Who is in determine-class roles? If the roles carrying the heaviest oversight burden are disproportionately held by any group, the burden is not equally distributed.

[8535] Effect of the junior-role finding. If entry-level roles are being reshaped, who currently holds them and who is affected by their redesign? This has a clear equality dimension and is the longest-lead item in the programme.

[8536] Language. Where the body has Welsh Language Standards obligations, the interface and any staff-facing materials fall within them.

[8537] Do not conclude "no impact". The honest finding is that the impact is real, differential and manageable — and that uniform friction is the version that fails the duty.

## Trade union engagement — a note to open the conversation [8539]

[8541] Draft for adaptation. Send before anything is built, not before it launches.

[8542] We are proposing to measure whether human oversight of AI systems in this service is working. We want to design it with you, and there is one design decision we would rather you set than we did.

[8543] The background: every instrument governing our use of AI treats human oversight as the main safeguard. None of them checks whether that safeguard is functioning. That is a risk to the public and, more immediately, a risk to members — because a colleague placed in an approval loop without the time, information or practised skill to exercise it meaningfully is not exercising accountability. They are absorbing liability for an institutional decision they could not realistically have controlled.

[8544] What we are proposing to measure: how the service as a whole is performing — how quickly outputs are approved, how much they are changed, whether errors are being caught.

[8545] What we are not proposing to measure, in any form: individual performance. There is no user identifier in the data schema. The schema is closed, so one cannot be added. The analysis tools refuse any query resolving to fewer than ten people, and refuse outright any file containing an identifier column. This is enforced in code rather than promised in policy, because we think a promise is worth less than a system that cannot do the thing.

[8546] What we would like to agree with you before we build: that this operates on a just-culture basis — closer to confidential safety reporting in aviation than to appraisal; that findings are never attributed, formally or informally; that participation in any unaided practice or sampling is scheduled work rather than an addition to workload; and that we jointly review, annually, whether any request for individual-level data has been made, and record that it was refused.

[8547] What we would ask in return: that where the measurement shows oversight is not working, the response is to fix the workload, the interface or the deployment — not the individual.

[8548] We would rather have this conversation now, at design stage, than present you with something finished. If the answer is that this cannot be made acceptable, we would rather know before we build it.

## Ethics application for canary injection — the content that will be asked for [8550]

[8552] Only needed at tier 3. Expect months, not weeks.

[8553] What is proposed. Injecting synthetic known-bad AI outputs, at a low randomised rate, into a live review queue, to measure whether reviewers detect them.

[8554] Why it cannot be done in a simulation. Detection under real time pressure, real caseload and real fatigue is the thing being measured. A laboratory version measures something else. This is the same reasoning behind live fire drills and phishing simulations, both of which have established precedent in government.

[8555] Harm to the public — the safety case. No canary can reach a citizen. Injected items are suppressed downstream by the platform regardless of the reviewer's disposition. State the technical mechanism, not the intention. Include the failure mode: what happens if the suppression fails, how it would be detected, and how quickly.

[8556] Harm to staff. Reviewers know canaries exist but not which items they are. The measure is aggregate and non-attributable; failing to catch one has no individual consequence and cannot be traced to a person. Address the stress question directly: this is a workload and design intervention if catch rates fall, not a disciplinary one.

[8557] Consent. Individual consent is not sought, for the same reason it is not sought for fire drills — announced tests measure announced behaviour. Collective agreement is sought instead, through the recognised unions, and staff are told the programme exists, its purpose, and that results are never individual.

[8558] Withdrawal. The union side can suspend injection. Say so explicitly; it is what makes the collective-agreement route legitimate.

[8559] Data. Canary events carry no identifier. Retention as per the DPIA.

[8560] Reporting. Aggregate catch rate by canary class, reported to the service owner and the SRO. Published internally including when results are poor.

[8561] The question the committee will ask: what happens if catch rates are very low? Answer in advance: it triggers a review of workload, interface and deployment scope — and, for a determine-class service, consideration of whether the deployment should continue in its current form. If you cannot commit to that, the case for injecting is weak.

## Governance templates — preamble [8563]

[8565] Four artefacts a department cannot deploy this without. Skeletons, not legal advice — take them to your DPO, equality lead and Government Legal Department contact. They exist so the conversation starts from a draft rather than a blank page.

## CONTRIBUTING.md [8567]

[8569] Run python3 -m pytest tests/ -q and python3 ../verify.py. Both must pass. CI runs them anyway.

[8570] Codes are additive and permanent. A code is never removed or repurposed; superseded codes are marked deprecated with a named successor. To propose an addition, give a definition, a worked example, and a statement of why an existing code does not fit.

[8571] Local codes must be prefixed x_. Anything unprefixed is reserved centrally so that local extension never collides with a future addition.

[8572] The schema is closed (additionalProperties: false) and contains no individual identifier field. Both properties are load-bearing: they are what makes the privacy commitment credible to staff and to unions rather than merely stated. A change that weakens either needs an explicit case, not a pull request.

[8573] Say what data the new threshold was calibrated against. Thresholds set by judgement should be labelled as such in the finding text, as the current ones are.

[8574] Prefer a test that would have caught a real defect. Every fix in the changelog was found by one of: a test, the verification harness, or a reader asking a sharp question. Only the first two scale.

## DEIA by default — who this serves, and the checklist [12175]

[12176] Every product must actively serve those experiencing the greatest adversity: economic hardship, disabled and neurodivergent users, underrepresented communities, vulnerable households and carers, digital exclusion and low literacy, and everyone algorithmic unfairness would otherwise reach first.

[12181] Who is most harmed if this fails or excludes?

[12185] Does the design assume internet access or literacy?

[12189] Has it been tested with people from affected groups?

[12193] Are legal obligations (Equality Act, PSED) documented?

[12197] Is there a non-digital fallback route?

[12201] Does the data we collect reflect the full population?

[12205] Are there language and accessibility alternatives?

[12209] How will we measure equitable outcomes, not just usage?

## Bias will be reproduced unless actively constrained [12211]

[12212] A model trained on historical outcomes learns the discrimination in the record, not the potential of a well-supported person. Four pre-specified bias domains to audit — and abstention ("insufficient data — human decision only") is always acceptable, and must be possible.

## Allocation [12215]

[12216] Systematically fewer or lesser recommendations for protected groups with equivalent profiles.

## Calibration [12218]

[12515] People and adoption · inclusion

## AI as assistive technology, designed for everyone [12516]

[12517] How AI tools help and hinder people across neurotypes at work, how to talk about them without a deficit framing, and the questions that are still open. Build one version that works for everyone, layered, rather than a separate one. From the Responsible AI and Data Use (RAIDU) work, merged into this playbook on 22 November 2026. Each item keeps its evidence grade: Proposed items are design proposals for review, not policy or established practice.

## What people say helps [12520]

## I like clear structure and knowing what to expect [12523]

[12524] “I want to know exactly what the tool will and won't do before I rely on it.”

[12525] Helps: Ask the tool to explain its steps before it does something complex; Build a short personal routine for how you use it, and stick to it

[12527] Watch for: Answers can vary between attempts — plan for that, it's not a fault

## Busy screens and long text wear me out fast [12530]

[12531] “Too much on the page at once and I lose track of what matters.”

[12532] Helps: Ask for short answers first, then "tell me more" only if needed; Turn off extra plug-ins or add-ons you don't use

[12534] Watch for: Take a proper break between tasks — don't stack requests back to back

## I want the tool to say exactly what it means [12537]

[12538] “I find it easier when nothing is left for me to guess or read between the lines.”

[12539] Helps: Ask it directly: "say this in plain, literal terms"; Ask it to list assumptions it's making, not just the answer

[12541] Watch for: General advice about people or feelings can be too generic — check it fits your actual situation

## My focus and energy shift a lot, hour to hour [12544]

[12545] “Some days I fly through things, other days the same task feels impossible.”

[12546] Helps: Let AI help you start a task — a blank page is often the hardest part; On a low-energy day, it's fine to lean on it more than usual

[12548] Watch for: On a good day, try the task yourself first — it keeps your own skill sharp

## I catch small details well, but time pressure throws me [12551]

[12552] “Give me time and I'll spot the error. Rush me and I'll miss it.”

[12553] Helps: Use AI for a fast first pass, then take your own unhurried time to check it; Ask it to flag its own uncertain bits so you know where to look closest

[12555] Watch for: Don't let a fast deadline push you into skipping your own check

## I feel uneasy sharing work before it's ready [12558]

[12559] “I'd rather get it right privately than be seen figuring it out.”

[12560] Helps: Use the tool as a private practice space before anything goes to a colleague; It's fine to use it purely to build confidence, not just to produce a final version

[12562] Watch for: Don't share more personal detail with it than the task actually needs

## Communicating about AI tools [12564]

[12566] Don't build two versions (one for neurodiverse staff, one for everyone else) . Managers' attitudes shaped use and control-group awareness was low; a split communication badges it as a 'special accommodation', undersells it to neurotypical staff and stigmatises it for neurodiverse staff.

[12568] Lead with the curb-cut framing, not the deficit framing . Outcome language ('levelled the playing field'), not diagnosis language. Avoid 'crutch' language even to knock it down.

[12570] Layer the detail rather than write two documents: a one-page plain-language summary with the fuller evidence base undern eath.

[12572] Talking to your manager: frame it in terms of outcome, not diagnosis ('this helps me structure written work faster and m ore confidently'); no need to disclose a condition; if it functions as a genuine accessibility aid, say so explicitly so it is treated like any reasonable adjustment if the licence is reviewed.

[12574] For managers: neutral, informed encouragement - not enthusiasm or scepticism - produces the best outcomes for the whole team.

[12576] one layout/format alone will not meet everyone's needs (some autism sub-types are polar oppos ites); present tailored around common characteristics or a compromise that best serves all; Easy Read version is a must. This partly overrides the turn-5 'one layered document' advice: the turn-11 solution is a characteristics poster plus a separate Easy Read version.

## Deployment and licensing [12578]

[12580] Don't blanket-licence . Target by task profile first, need second (admin-heavy/high-information roles benefited; Legal and Policy did not).

[12582] Fund self-led exploration over formal training sessions; budget time, not just courseware (p < 0 .01 at 2+ hours self-led use).

[12584] Plan continuity, not just onboarding . If a licence functions as assistive technology for someone, treat withdrawal with the same seriousness as withdrawing any other reasonable adjustment, not as an IT asset reclaim.

[12586] Build QA expectations that vary by task, not a blanket 'always check' policy nobody follows . Drafting/summarising: light-touch spot-check. Data analysis and anything feeding a decision: mandate verification (DBT observed tasks showed Copilot users did worse on Excel analysis).

[12588] Track dependency alongside satisfaction in any evaluation commissioned; none of the three government evaluations measure d these jointly at individual level - a genuine gap.

[12590] Cost transparency matters to uptake: address ethical/environmental concerns rather than dismiss them .

## Keeping research current [12592]

[12594] Model-dependent findings Describe a specific model's failure mode at a specific point in time (e.g. 2024 ChatGPT advising an autistic user to 'just walk up and start talking'). Testable claims, not settled facts. Re-run the equivalent prompt against current models before relying on it (five-minute check). Tag [model-dependent — re-verify before citing]; note model and test date; anything older than about six months needs a fresh spot-check.

[12596] Structural (human-factors and organisational) findings About people and institutions, not the model. Safe to build governance policy on now. Tag [structural — durable].

[12598] More fluent models are more persuasive when wrong Newer, more fluent, more agreeable models are not guaranteed to reduce dependency risk — they may increase it, because a model better at sounding authoritative and more consistently agreeable is more persuasive when wrong. 'The tooling has evolved' is a reason to scrutinise sycophancy and over-reliance harder, not to trust more.

## Open questions [12600]

[12602] Is chatbot-based support for autistic people legitimate assistive technology, or a paternalistic fix aimed at the wrong target? For: Autistic users in the CMU study chose this themselves, unprompted by clinicians, because existing workplace support was inadequate or absent — 'it's the only thing I trust.' Respecting autonomy means respecting that choice, not gatekeeping it behind professional approval. Against: A review Begel co-authored found 90% of HRI research on autism excluded autistic perspectives — a documented history of building 'solutions' nobody with autism wanted. Chatbot advice-giving individualises a structural workplace-inclusion failure: asking an autistic employee to get better at masking via AI coaching instead of making the workplace accessible treats the symptom.

[12604] Does satisfaction without measured productivity gain justify public licensing spend? For: DBT frames wellbeing, confidence and inclusion as legitimate outcomes independent of output volume; a more sustainable, less anxious workforce is a defensible use of public money, especially for a protected characteristic. Against: DBT's own conclusion: no evidence time savings led to improved productivity; value for money unassessed. Licences justified by self-reported satisfaction are weak in any Treasury-facing review and risk being read as subsidised comfort.

[12606] Does normalising AI-mediated compensation reduce institutional pressure to provide genuine accommodation? For: (risk is real) If AI drafting becomes the default fix for a dyslexic employee, the organisation has less incentive to fund proper adjustments, job redesign or human support - AI is cheaper and needs no line-management change. Against: Assumes accommodation is zero-sum; DBT and Capita evidence shows the tool works alongside existing adjustments and often surfaces previously invisible/unfunded need - additive, not replacement.

[12608] Universal rollout versus targeted, disclosure-based provisioning? For: (universal) Curb-cut argument: benefits accrue to non-native English speakers, hearing- and vision-impaired staff and many neurotypical staff (80% of use cases rated satisfactory across DBT). Targeting requires disclosure, which carries stigma risk (CMU respondents worried). Against: Untargeted rollout produced DBT's finding that Legal and Policy roles got minor benefit while absorbing the same licence cost and verification burden; also removes a comparison group, making it harder to tell real accessibility benefit from placebo/novelty.

[12610] Is self-report evidence trustworthy? For: Confidence, cognitive load and satisfaction are inherently subjective - self-report is the correct instrument. DBT triangulated with interviews and observed tasks and found broadly consistent patterns. Against: Respondents volunteered (70% of DBT) or knew they were evaluated on a tool their employer promoted - social-desirability and novelty bias. The only non-self-report measure (observed tasks) contradicted diary data on Excel analysis and PowerPoint quality.

[12612] Is it responsible to act on this evidence at all, given how fast tooling changes? For: (act now) Waiting for model-current research means never acting. Structural findings (manager influence, training modality, compensatory-vs-substitutive risk) are durable - acting on those is low-risk. Against: The most policy-relevant claims (advice quality, hallucination frequency, persuasiveness/over-reliance risk) are model-dependent and most likely wrong by the time a document reaches a minister. Citing a 2024 finding as current without re-testing is a factual risk.

## Product documentation [13711]

[13720] Delivery documentation · PRD

## Product requirements [13721]

[13722] What this guide is for, who it serves, what it must do and what it deliberately does not do. Derived from published guidance and community discussion; a proposal, not an adopted product mandate.

## Problems worth solving [13724]

[13725] Each problem is visible in the source material rather than assumed.

## Guidance is real but scattered [13727]

[13728] The AI Playbook, Service Standard, TCoP, ATRS, NCSC secure-AI guidelines, ethics frameworks and FinOps practice exist separately. Teams reassemble them from scratch, inconsistently, each time.

## Experimentation outruns governance [13730]

[13731] Personal assistants become shared agents and then business-critical dependencies without registration, named ownership, assurance or funded support.

## Cost is discussed as licences [13733]

[13734] Token and licence spend is visible; data remediation, workflow redesign, assurance, human review, monitoring, support and exit are not costed or owned.

## Evidence is claimed, not demonstrated [13736]

[13737] The same product yields different results under different evaluation methods, so headline productivity figures travel further than the method that produced them.

## Community knowledge decays [13739]

[13740] Sessions, transcripts, repositories and personal networks hold the learning; there is no shared discovery layer, taxonomy or evidence pack, so lessons are relearned.

## Goals and how each is judged [13741]

## One route from mandate to governed operation [13744]

[13745] A reader can go from no policy position to a registered, assured, monitored agent using only this guide.

[13753] Criticality drives the gate; low-risk work stays fast.

[13757] Claims carry method, publisher and date; illustrative material is labelled.

[13785] Issuing approvals or acting as the assurance authority

[13787] Replacing or overriding central or departmental guidance

## Non-functional requirements [13788]

[13793] Accessibility WCAG 2.2 AA: contrast, focus visibility, keyboard operation, reduced-motion, semantic headings and labels.

[13795] Information handling OFFICIAL working content only. No personal data, no case data, no credentials. Assessment answers stay on the reader's device.

## Low-level design [14263]

[14264] Module responsibilities, the arithmetic behind every score, the validation rules and the accessibility implementation. Enough for someone else to rebuild the behaviour exactly.

## Modules and their state [14266]

## Navigation module [14269]

[14271] groupDefs → flat chapter list → numbering, accents, prev/next, contents

[14273] section, groups, read, toc

[14274] Barometer module eight dimension scores → mean → band with colour and label scores (persisted)

[14278] Criticality module ten dimension scores → total → tier and gate mapping crit, gateTier

[14282] Barrier module impact × likelihood → 1–25 → four bands bar

## Economics module [14288]

[14290] tokens = words ÷ 0.75; cost = in×priceIn + out×priceOut + tools + infra + review

[14292] lab, ue

[14293] Instruction module seven fields → composed block → clipboard blk, copied

## Algorithms [14297]

## Barometer banding [14299]

[14300] mean of rated dimensions; 0–0.9 Nascent, 1.0–1.9 Emerging, 2.0–2.4 Establishing, 2.5–3.0 Leading; unrated dimensions excluded from the mean and reported as unrated.

## Criticality to gate [14302]

[14303] sum of ten dimensions scored 1–5; 10–20 personal, 21–30 team, 31–38 departmental, 39–44 operational service, 45–50 citizen impact.

## Barrier banding [14305]

[14306] impact × likelihood on 1–5 scales; 1–3 low, 4–8 medium, 9–15 high, 16–25 critical.

## Unit economics [14308]

[14309] value per interaction = (minutes saved ÷ 60 × hourly rate) × quality factor; net = value − cost; return = net ÷ cost expressed as a percentage.

## Validation rules [14312]

[14313] Numeric inputs Clamp to declared minimum and maximum; reject non-numeric silently rather than throwing.

[14315] Unrated dimensions Show an em dash, never a zero, and exclude from means.

[14317] Currency Two decimal places, pound sign, thousands separated; never rounded away in totals.

[14319] Clipboard Plain text only; confirm with a transient state, no alert.

[14321] Persistence One key, versioned; parse defensively and fall back to blank on any error.

## Accessibility implementation [14324]

[14325] Colour Every text and meaningful non-text pair contrast-tested; accents have separate text-safe variants where a fill carries text.

[14327] Keyboard All controls are buttons or inputs; aria-pressed and aria-current reflect state; focus ring never suppressed.

[14329] Motion The guidance ticker pauses on hover and respects prefers-reduced-motion.

[14331] Structure One h1 per chapter, sequential headings, aria-labels on sections, skip link to content.

[14333] Language British English, plain terms, expanded acronyms on first use in a chapter.

## Director or SRO, accounting-officer line [14457]
