## User stories with acceptance criteria [14545]

[14547] As a Accountable leader , I need to see the method behind any productivity claim, so that I do not repeat an unevidenced figure in public.

[14549] Accepted when: Every figure shows publisher, date and method, or is labelled illustrative

[14551] As a Accountable leader , I need to know which agents are high risk and who owns them, so that I can direct attention where consequence is highest.

[14553] Accepted when: Control tower lists risk level, owner and next review per agent

[14555] As a Service owner , I need to know the gate an agent must pass before it touches my service, so that I can plan assurance rather than discover it.

[14557] Accepted when: Criticality score returns a tier with named evidence and review frequency

[14559] As a Service owner , I need to have an exit path for a platform or model, so that a supplier change does not stop my service.

[14561] Accepted when: Seven-step exit path with the dependencies it addresses

[14563] As a AI engineer , I need to decide where grounding information should live, so that I do not create ungoverned copies.

[14565] Accepted when: Decision tree returns one of four options in priority order

[14567] As a AI engineer , I need to compose an instruction block once and reuse it, so that behaviour is consistent across platforms.

[14569] Accepted when: Seven-part block copies out as plain text

[14571] As a Assurance specialist , I need to score criticality across ten dimensions, so that control is proportionate to consequence.

[14573] Accepted when: Score maps to one of five gates with its controls

[14575] As a Assurance specialist , I need to record transparency information for every internal agent, so that oversight and audit have something to inspect.

[14577] Accepted when: Eight-section ATRS record with all fields listed

[14579] As a FinOps lead , I need to model cost per run and per month, so that a business case includes consumption, not guesses.

[14581] Accepted when: Cost lab returns per-run and monthly figures with a language multiplier

[14583] As a FinOps lead , I need to see value against cost per interaction, so that I can show whether the agent earns its keep.

[14585] Accepted when: Unit economics returns value, net and return

[14587] As a Frontline practitioner , I need to know what I may use and when to escalate, so that I can work confidently within the guardrails.

[14589] Accepted when: Support chapter states allowed use, escalation and where help comes from

[14591] As a Community manager , I need to turn a session into a reusable evidence pack, so that learning survives the meeting.

[14593] Accepted when: Evidence pack structure with owner, taxonomy and review date

## Journeys [14594]

## First-time reader to first decision [14595]

[14598] Arrives with a question Lands on the overview, sees proposal status “Is this authoritative?” Proposal flag and hierarchy answer it in one screen

[14602] Finds the applicable chapter Uses search or contents “Where does my case sit?” Chapter numbering and part accents orient quickly

[14606] Runs an assessment Tier finder or criticality radar “Am I over- or under-controlling?” Tier arrives with evidence and review expectations

[14610] Takes an artefact away Copies the register schema or instruction block “What do I do on Monday?” Copyable artefacts, not prose

[14614] Returns for oversight Re-opens the control tower and maturity evidence “Has anything drifted?” Read state and review cadence bring them back

## Agent from idea to retirement [14617]

[14620] Idea Someone builds a helpful agent “This saves me an hour a day” Register at creation, not at scale

[14624] Share Colleagues start relying on it “It works, so why formalise it?” Promotion gate between personal and team scope

[14628] Assure Criticality scored, tier applied “How much control is proportionate?” Gate names the evidence needed

[14632] Operate Monitoring, cost and quality watched “Who notices if it degrades?” Named owner and continuous duties

[14636] Review Re-authorise, improve, restrict or retire “Is it still earning its authority?” Review date forces the decision

[14640] Retire Access revoked, records archived “What happens to the evidence?” Archive and audit stage in the lifecycle

## Community session to reused pattern [14643]

[14646] Session happens Weekly call, recorded from 17 August 2026 “Will I find this again?” Automatic recording closes part of the capture gap

[14650] Capture Transcript, chat, files, commitments “Who owns the follow-up?” Session evidence pack with owner and actions

[14654] Classify Taxonomy: capability, use case, sensitivity, owner, review date “Which of these applies to me?” Shared taxonomy across communities

[14658] Connect Federated index links to governed sources “Is this the current version?” Index links rather than copies

[14662] Reuse Another organisation adopts the pattern “Has anyone tried this already?” Discovery by role, sector, maturity and supplier

[14666] Learn Outcome and corrections returned “Did it actually work?” Value reported as reuse, not attendance

## Service blueprint — an agent in an operational service [14669]

[14670] Five lanes across the same five moments: what the user does, what they see, what happens behind it, what supports it, and what is recorded.

## User actions [14672]

[14673] Requests help Reviews agent output Accepts or challenges Escalates an error Feeds back on value

## Frontstage [14680]

[14681] Agent responds with citation Confidence and limits shown Human review point Escalation route offered Feedback captured in service

## Backstage [14688]

[14689] Retrieval over authoritative sources Guardrails and permission checks Logging and audit trail Incident triage and rollback Evaluation against baseline

## Supporting processes [14696]

[14697] Register and ATRS record maintained Assurance gate evidence held Cost allocated to the use case Supplier and model change managed Review or retirement decision

## Evidence and records [14704]

[14705] Source provenance Approval and sign-off Monitoring and drift reports Incident records Benefit evidence

# Reference

[Open this section on the publisher’s website](https://cyberdudeuk.github.io/ai-capability-governance/#part-reference)

The numbers in brackets identify elements in the ordered DOM inventory. This is a text projection of Em’s material.

## Reference [15701]

[15710] Pan-UK

## All four nations have strategy. One has published evaluation. [15711]

[15712] Counting strategies overstates maturity: a benchmark that measures published strategy ranks all four nations comparable. Only one has a published body of controlled evaluation of deployment. What each nation can borrow from the others is the point of comparing.

## UK Government [15716]

[15717] England and reserved functions

[15718] Strategy

[15786] International

## Benchmarking the UK's position [15787]

[15788] Five reference jurisdictions, five different bets: from the EU's binding risk tiers to Singapore's testing-led pragmatism. Genuinely transferable: Canada's public assessment and inventory approach, Australia's named AI ownership and workforce model, Singapore's central adoption flywheel, US inventory discipline, and the EU's joint procurement direction.

[15791] Where Key instrument Model For public bodies

## UK [15798]

[15800] AI Playbook + sector regulators; ATRS; AI Security Institute evaluations

[15802] Principles-led, pro-innovation; non-statutory for now

[15804] Playbook principles and ATRS records; four published evaluations; frontier legislation under consideration

## EU [15807]

[15809] AI Act (in force 1 Aug 2024; Digital Omnibus 2026 defers high-risk duties to Dec 2027, public authorities to Aug 2030); EuropAI joint procurement

[15811] Binding, risk-based regulation

[15813] High-risk public deployments: conformity assessment, logging, human oversight, fundamental-rights impact assessment

## US [15816]

[15818] NIST AI Risk Management Framework; OMB memoranda; GAO oversight

[15820] Voluntary framework + agency rules; state laws vary

[15822] Federal AI use-case inventories and Chief AI Officers; rapid growth with persistent policy and budget challenges

## Canada [15825]

[15827] Directive on Automated Decision-Making + Algorithmic Impact Assessment; agentic-AI guidance (May 2026)

[15829] Binding on federal automated decisions

[15831] Mandatory AIA before deployment; names skill atrophy as an oversight risk; bounded autonomy and recoverability

## Singapore [15834]

[15836] Model AI Governance Framework · AI Verify toolkit

[15838] Voluntary, testing-led

[15840] Central funding, shared platforms, problem intake, applied learning — an adoption flywheel

## The EU AI Act's four risk tiers [15842]

[15843] In force 1 August 2024. The Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026) moved stand-alone high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027, embedded high-risk systems to 2 August 2028 and high-risk systems for public authorities to 2 August 2030. Article 50 transparency duties have applied since 2 August 2026. Obligations follow the use case, not the technology. The benchmark other regimes are measured against.

[15846] Unacceptable

[15847] Banned outright: social scoring, subliminal manipulation, real-time remote biometric ID in public spaces (narrow exceptions).

[15849] High risk

[15850] Essential public services, law enforcement, employment, critical infrastructure: conformity assessment, documentation, human oversight, EU database registration.

[15852] Limited risk

[15853] Transparency duties: chatbots must say they are AI; synthetic media must be labelled.

[15855] Minimal risk

[15856] Most systems: spam filters, recommenders. No mandatory obligations; voluntary codes encouraged.

## The supranational layer [15857]

## OECD AI Principles + OECD.AI Observatory [15860]

[15861] The shared definition of AI used by the UK Playbook and the EU AI Act. The OECD.AI Policy Observatory tracks national AI policies worldwide; it is the model for this app's observatory.

## Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (2024) [15863]

[15864] The first binding international AI treaty: human rights, democracy and the rule of law. The UK is a signatory.

## G7 Hiroshima AI Process (2023) [15866]

[15867] International guiding principles and a code of conduct for organisations developing advanced AI systems.

## AI Safety Summit series: Bletchley, Seoul, Paris [15869]

[15870] Frontier-safety declarations and the network of national AI safety and security institutes. Started at Bletchley Park, November 2023.

## UN General Assembly resolution (2024) [15872]

[15873] First UN consensus resolution on safe, secure and trustworthy AI for sustainable development.

[15886] Reference · pace and parity

## Named once. Controlled nowhere. [15887]

[15888] Skill atrophy appears in this guide as a single sentence in the evidence chapter, credited to Canada. Nothing sits behind it: no control, no metric, no register field, no gate criterion, no owner. That is the honest answer to the question, and it is now backlog item PACE-01 . This chapter closes it, then applies the same test to everything else the world has built that we have not.

[15893] Named

## Yes [15894]

[15895] One sentence, evidence chapter, attributed to Canada

[15897] Controlled

## No [15898]

[15899] No control, no owner, no frequency

[15901] Measured

## No [15902]

[15903] No metric in the barometer or control tower

[15905] Gated

## No [15906]

[15907] No criterion in the quality gate

## What Canada actually did [15908]

[15909] Six moves, and the last is the operable one. The instrument is the Guide on the Use of Agentic Artificial Intelligence, published by the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat on 22 May 2026, sitting on top of a directive that already made assessment mandatory.

## Named the risk inside an instrument [15912]

[15913] Continued offloading of decisions to AI agents can lead to knowledge and skill atrophy and weakened human judgment. Employees become less practiced at core tasks and slower to notice when something is wrong.

[15914] Guide on the Use of Agentic AI, TBS, 22 May 2026

## Tied it to the validity of oversight [15916]

[15917] Maintenance of relevant skill sets among agentic AI users and deployers is treated as a prerequisite for meaningful human oversight. Not a wellbeing concern — a validity condition on the control itself.

[15918] Same instrument, mitigations

## Added two agent-specific principles [15920]

[15921] Bounded autonomy and recoverability, introduced alongside the existing generative-AI principles rather than replacing them.

[15922] Same instrument

## Named the consequence chain [15924]

[18007] Mandatory for UK central government annual reports: departments, agencies and NDPBs report ICT and digital waste by destination and footprint by device category. Data centre emissions count as Scope 1/2 if you own or control the data centre, otherwise Scope 3, and are 'material-only' reporting – so cloud-hosted AI compute is not a minimum reporting line. Caveat: No AI-specific content; last part of the page (about 12% of text) not read.

[18009] HM Treasury

[18010] Sustainability Reporting Guidance 2025-26 (opens an external website)

[18014] Greening Government: ICT and Digital Services Strategy 2020-2025 and successor

[18015] UK-wide . Policy, Unconfirmed

[18017] The 2020-25 strategy set five ICT sustainability objectives to March 2025; the 2024-25 annual report (July 2026) says most were on track. A UK government digital sustainability strategy led by Defra is promised but not published as at the latest sources, and Government Buying Standards are to gain ICT sustainability criteria. Until then there is no government-wide target for AI energy or water use. Caveat: Successor strategy status unconfirmed; Defra digital sustainability blog (26 March 2026) described it as upcoming. Neither source mentions AI energy or water.

[18019] Defra

[18020] Greening Government Commitments ICT annual report 2024 to 2025 (opens an external website)

[18024] Using AI ethically and sustainably (draft AI Knowledge Hub guidance)

[18025] UK-wide . Guidance, Draft

[18027] Draft civil-service guidance: first ask whether AI is needed at all, then choose the smallest model that can do the job, keep prompts short and avoid unnecessary back-and-forth. This is the clearest government steer towards routing work to cheaper, lower-energy models, which also reduces cost. Caveat: Seen only via a secondary report (XenoSpectrum, 29 Sept 2026) of a page on a 'dev' domain marked draft; not verified directly. Gives no measured energy or water figures.

[18029] Cabinet Office AI policy / GDS (unconfirmed)

[18030] Using AI ethically and sustainably (draft) (opens an external website)

[18034] Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009, s.44 public bodies duties

[18035] Scotland . Law, In force

[18037] Scottish public bodies must act in the way best calculated to help meet Scotland's emissions targets, help deliver the climate change adaptation programme, and act most sustainably. Annual reporting is required under the 2015 Order. Large AI and cloud contracts should therefore be appraised for emissions. Caveat: In force since 1 January 2011. The reporting Order (SSI 2015/347) and its later amendments were not re-checked.

[18039] Scottish Government

[18040] Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009, section 44 (opens an external website)

[18044] Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015

[18045] Wales . Law, In force

[18047] Named Welsh public bodies have a well-being duty (s.3) to act in line with the sustainable development principle towards the seven well-being goals (s.4). AI investment decisions, including their long-term costs and environmental impacts, should be framed against these goals. Caveat: The Welsh public sector's 2030 net zero collective ambition and Net Zero Reporting Guide were seen only through a 2022 trade article – not verified.

[18049] Welsh Government

[18050] Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 (opens an external website)

## Transparency and automated decisions (9) [18053]

[18058] Obligation

[18059] Where, kind and status

[18060] What it means for AI use

[18061] Owner

[18062] Basis

[18065] The Judge Over Your Shoulder (JOYS)

[18066] England and Wales . Guidance, Current

[18068] The Government Legal Department's guide to the public law principles that decision-makers must follow: legality, rationality, procedural fairness and proper consideration. These apply equally when AI or automated tools support a decision, so officials must be able to explain and justify AI-assisted decisions and must not unlawfully fetter their discretion. Caveat: The landing page does not mention automated decision-making or AI; applying JOYS to AI is an interpretation. Scotland has a separate judicial review system; extent shown reflects the English courts focus and should be checked.

[18070] Government Legal Department

[18071] The Judge Over Your Shoulder (6th edition) (opens an external website)

[18075] Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) - mandatory scope

[18076] UK-wide . Standard, In force

[18078] Central government departments and arm's-length bodies that deliver public services or interact with the public must publish an ATRS record for algorithmic tools that significantly influence decisions with public effect or interact directly with the public, once the tool reaches beta, pilot or production. Retired tools need their record marked 'Retired'; FOI or data protection exemptions can justify marking fields 'EXEMPT'. Caveat: Policy, not statute. Page metadata shows an update on 9-10 September 2026 with no change note. Ownership after July 2026 not formally confirmed.

[18080] Government Digital Service (published under DSIT; GDS now in DCMS) (DSIT, abolished 21 July 2026; check the successor owner)

[18081] Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard: mandatory scope and exemptions policy (opens an external website)

[18085] ATRS for the wider public sector (local government, devolved bodies)

[18086] UK-wide . Standard, Current

[18088] Outside central government, ATRS is recommended but not required. It is endorsed by the Data Standards Authority, and the stated intent is to extend the requirement across the broader public sector over time. Councils and other bodies can publish records voluntarily. Caveat: No date has been set for extending the requirement. The MHCLG Local AI plans of July 2026 do not mention ATRS.

[18090] Government Digital Service / Data Standards Authority

[18091] ATRS mandatory scope and exemptions policy; ATRS hub (opens an external website)

[18095] Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 - automated decision-making (section 80, UK GDPR Articles 22A-22D)

[18096] UK-wide . Law, In force

[18098] From 5 February 2026, significant decisions based solely on automated processing can rely on a wider range of lawful bases, but safeguards are mandatory. People must be told about the decision and be able to make representations, get human intervention and contest it. Decisions based on special category data are restricted. The changes do not apply to decisions taken before 5 February 2026. Caveat: Commenced by SI 2026/82 (made 29 Jan 2026). The data subject complaints provisions (s.103) commenced 19 June 2026.

[18100] Parliament; regulated by the ICO

[18101] The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 6 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/82) (opens an external website)

[18105] ICO guidance on automated decision-making and profiling (DUAA update)

[18106] UK-wide . Guidance, Consultation

[18108] Draft ICO guidance explains when processing counts as solely automated decision-making with legal or similarly significant effects, and what safeguards are needed. Meaningful human involvement means an active review by someone with the authority and competence to change the outcome, before the decision is final, and it should be recorded. Public task is likely the relevant lawful basis for public bodies. Caveat: Consultation ran 31 March to 29 May 2026; final version not confirmed as published by 19 Oct 2026. The earlier version remains in use until the update is finalised.

[18110] Information Commissioner's Office

[18111] Automated decision-making, including profiling (draft for consultation) (opens an external website)

[18115] ICO statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making

[18116] UK-wide . Regulation, Draft

[18118] Regulations require the Information Commissioner to prepare a statutory code of practice on processing personal data when developing and using AI and automated decision-making. Once in force, courts and the ICO must take it into account, so public bodies deploying AI should expect it to become the main data protection benchmark. Caveat: Secondary commentary (Arnold & Porter) says the Regulations came into force on 12 May 2026 and the code is not expected to take effect until 2027; the made and in-force dates were not visible on the legislation page.

[18120] Information Commissioner's Office

[18121] The Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/425) (opens an external website)

[18125] Data and AI Ethics Framework and self-assessment tool

[18126] UK-wide . Framework, Current

[18128] Teams designing, building, buying or running data and AI projects in the public sector should use this framework. It has seven principles: fairness, accountability and transparency, plus privacy, environmental sustainability, societal impact and safety, added in December 2025. Its self-assessment tool records decisions and trade-offs. Caveat: Retitled from 'Data Ethics Framework' on 18 December 2025; first published 2018.

[18130] Government Digital Service (now in DCMS)

[18131] Data and AI Ethics Framework (opens an external website)

[18135] Scottish AI Register

[18136] Scotland . Register, Current

[18138] This is a public register of AI systems used or developed by the Scottish Government and the wider Scottish public sector. Registration is mandatory for the Scottish Government and its core agencies; other public bodies are encouraged to register now, with mandatory registration planned in phases. Register any qualifying system and keep its lifecycle stage up to date. Caveat: Mandatory scope comes from a March/April 2024 announcement and a Data Lab case study (2026). The Digital Strategy delivery plan (Nov 2025) refers only to 'continued use' and does not state a mandate. No date has been found for extending the requirement beyond core Scottish Government. The register website could not be fetched.

[18140] Scottish Government (developed with the Scottish AI Alliance)

[18141] Scottish AI Register (Data Ethics Guidance listing); Scottish AI Alliance 5-year case study (opens an external website)

[18145] Public Law Project - Tracking Automated Government (TAG) register

[18146] UK-wide . Register, Current

[18148] A civil-society register of automated and algorithmic tools used by UK public bodies, compiled from FOI and other sources. It is not an official record, but it shows the outside scrutiny your tool may face and can help identify comparable systems and legal challenges. Caveat: Secondary, non-official source. Launch date and current coverage not verified in this check.

[18150] Public Law Project (charity)

[18151] The Tracking Automated Government register (opens an external website)

## Value and benefits (6) [18154]

[18159] Obligation

[18160] Where, kind and status

[18161] What it means for AI use

[18162] Owner

[18163] Basis

[18166] NAO: Use of artificial intelligence in government (2024)

[18167] UK-wide . Guidance, Current

[18169] The National Audit Office found 37% of 87 responding bodies had deployed AI (typically one or two use cases) and 70% were piloting or planning it. It said the draft AI adoption strategy lacked performance metrics, an implementation plan and clear ownership, and did not set out how benefits would be measured. Expect auditors to ask for baseline and benefits evidence. Caveat: Based on a 2023 survey; adoption has moved on since.

[18171] National Audit Office

[18172] Use of artificial intelligence in government (opens an external website)

[18176] Public Accounts Committee: Use of AI in Government (HC 356)

[18177] UK-wide . Guidance, Current

[18179] The PAC's 18th report of 2024-26 (26 March 2025) followed the NAO work. Government's follow-up letter (18 November 2025) committed to consistent metrics for legacy technology costs and the cost of not acting, tracking remediation funding, and milestones and measures in the digital and AI roadmap – with deadlines moved into mid-2026. Caveat: Report conclusions not read in full; points taken from the government's November 2025 progress letter. Delivery status of the mid-2026 commitments unconfirmed.

[18181] House of Commons Public Accounts Committee

[18182] 18th Report – Use of AI in Government

[18184] NAO: Good practice guide for organisations using AI

[18185] UK-wide . Guidance, Current

[18187] The NAO warns that AI productivity promises are 'not yet borne out by real world experience' – faster individual tasks do not automatically raise throughput where approvals and governance slow work. It asks for measurable objectives, clear pilot success criteria and committed funding, and flags dependence on large external suppliers and cloud providers. Caveat: Published May 2026 (exact day not shown). No cost framework and no environmental content.

[18189] National Audit Office

[18190] Good practice guide for organisations using AI (opens an external website)

[18194] NAO: Improving government's productivity through better cost information

[18195] UK-wide . Guidance, Current

[18197] Departments know total running costs but often lack activity-level cost information, so they cannot target expensive areas or prove productivity gains. The NAO recommends named senior owners for services and simple methods to measure staff time on activities – the baseline you need to show whether AI actually reduces cost per case. In February 2026 the Comptroller and Auditor General publicly questioned whether Copilot licences were delivering gains that justified their cost. Caveat: Copilot remark reported by a trade publication (11 Feb 2026), not an NAO report finding.

[18199] National Audit Office

[18200] Improving government's productivity through better cost information (opens an external website)

[18204] Microsoft 365 Copilot experiment: cross-government findings

[18205] UK-wide, Wales . Guidance, Current

[18207] About 20,000 staff in 12 organisations (including the Welsh Government) used M365 Copilot from September to December 2024. Users self-reported an average saving of 26 minutes a day; 17% saw no clear saving. The report includes no costs or return-on-investment analysis and could not say how saved time was used, so it cannot on its own justify licence spend. Caveat: Time savings are self-reported from range midpoints. DWP's separate Copilot trial evaluation (29 Jan 2026) exists, but its methods and figures were not read.

[18209] Government Digital Service (DCMS)

[18210] Microsoft 365 Copilot Experiment: Cross-Government Findings Report (opens an external website)

[18214] Magenta Book: Guidance on the impact evaluation of AI interventions

[18215] UK-wide . Guidance, Current

[18217] HM Treasury and Evaluation Task Force guidance: plan baselines and a comparison group before deploying AI, and strongly consider randomising access, timing or encouragement because AI is delivered digitally; otherwise use quasi-experimental designs. Its case study cautions against extrapolating early time savings to the whole civil service. Caveat: Last updated 15 May 2026; final part of the page not read.

[18219] HM Treasury; Evaluation Task Force

[18220] Guidance on the Impact Evaluation of AI Interventions (opens an external website)

## Workforce and skills (7) [18223]

[18228] Obligation

[18229] Where, kind and status

[18230] What it means for AI use

[18231] Owner

[18232] Basis

[18235] One Big Thing 2025: AI for All

[18236] UK-wide . Practice, Current

[18238] Every civil servant was asked to complete about one hour of foundational, responsible-use AI training (four 15-minute modules on Civil Service Learning) and take part in departmental activities. Check your department's One Big Thing hub for approved tools and local rules. Caveat: Participation by devolved civil services varies. Wales's Strategic AI Advisory Group discussed it in November 2025; Scottish Government and NICS participation was not confirmed.

[18240] Cabinet Office (Modern Civil Service)

[18241] One Big Thing: AI for All is live (opens an external website)

[18245] Government Skills: Artificial intelligence skills for all

[18246] UK-wide . Guidance, Current

[18248] Free AI courses on Civil Service Learning at four levels: awareness (AI Fundamentals), working (ethics, business value, generative AI), practitioner (machine learning, NLP, working with LLMs) and a two-part Senior Civil Service pathway. Copilot learning is in the Digital skills for all curriculum.

[18249] Government Skills (Cabinet Office)

[18250] Artificial intelligence skills for all (opens an external website)

[18254] Workforce Partnership Council: Managing technology that manages people / Using AI at work

[18255] Wales . Guidance, Current

[18257] Social partnership guidance agreed by the Welsh Government, public sector employers and trade unions. It requires human oversight of strategic decisions and human involvement in day-to-day decisions made by algorithmic management systems. It also calls for consultation and procurement due diligence, staff training, ongoing monitoring and protection of individual rights when AI is used to manage staff. Caveat: Guidance, not statute. It sits within the social partnership model, but its link to the duties in the Social Partnership and Public Procurement (Wales) Act 2023 was not confirmed.

[18259] Welsh Government Workforce Partnership Council (Welsh Government, unions, employers)

[18260] Wales' public sector leading the way in responsible AI use (opens an external website)

[18264] Social Partnership and Public Procurement (Wales) Act 2023

[18265] Wales . Law, In force

[18267] Sets up the Social Partnership Council and a social partnership duty requiring listed Welsh public bodies to seek consensus or compromise with recognised trade unions when setting well-being objectives and making decisions of a strategic nature. It also creates a socially responsible procurement duty. It is the statutory basis for involving unions in strategic AI workforce decisions in Wales. Caveat: The Act does not mention AI; applying it to AI is an interpretation. The summary of the duty is from general knowledge of the Act and was not re-read in section text during this check. Royal Assent date not shown on the contents page.

[18269] Welsh Government; Social Partnership Council

[18270] Social Partnership and Public Procurement (Wales) Act 2023 (opens an external website)

[18274] PCS demands for a civil service AI agreement

[18275] UK-wide . Practice, Current

[18277] PCS, the largest civil service union, wants formal talks with the Cabinet Office on AI. Its demands include agreement before AI systems are introduced, disclosure of existing systems, no AI decisions about staff or AI monitoring of workers, no job losses, impact assessments before roll-out and shared productivity gains. Expect these points in departmental consultations on AI. Caveat: Union position, not an obligation.

[18279] Public and Commercial Services Union

[18280] PCS calls for formal talks with Cabinet Office on AI (opens an external website)

[18284] FDA and Fabian Society: Adopt, Innovate, Transform

[18285] UK-wide . Practice, Current

[18287] The senior civil servants' union and the Fabian Society call for an AI vision developed with staff and unions, better access to AI tools, and AI career paths and reward. They also want AI protections agreed with unions, including ways for staff to give feedback on how AI is used. Caveat: Union and think-tank position, not an obligation.

[18289] FDA (union) and Fabian Society

[18290] FDA and Fabian Society launch new AI report (opens an external website)

[18294] TUC Artificial Intelligence (Regulation and Employment Rights) Bill campaign

[18295] UK-wide . Practice, Current

[18297] The TUC has drafted a 'ready to go' AI bill that would require workers to be told when AI makes important decisions about them, give a right to an explanation and keep decisions human-centred. It has no legal force, but it frames union expectations for AI used in HR, pay, discipline and monitoring. Caveat: Campaign document. Page last modified 11 Nov 2025. No government bill has adopted it.

[18299] Trades Union Congress

[18300] Launching the TUC's 'Ready to Go' AI Bill (opens an external website)

# Start here

[Open this section on the publisher’s website](https://cyberdudeuk.github.io/ai-capability-governance/#part-start-here)

The numbers in brackets identify elements in the ordered DOM inventory. This is a text projection of Em’s material.

[1539] Part 1 of 12 · 5 chapters

## Start here [1540]

## AI Capability Governance and Implementation [1549]

[1550] The guidance for deploying AI agents in the public sector, sequenced into one route — and the operating capability that turns experimentation into governed services. Crown-copyright sources are the government's own; every illustrative figure is labelled.

## Start here [1556]

[1557] Eight stages from mandate to governed operation. The last stage feeds the third: every review either re-authorises the agent, changes it, or ends it.

## Stage 8 returns to stage 3 — the loop does not close [1561]

[1564] Usage and cost Who uses it, how often, what it spends

[1567] Accuracy and drift Evaluation results against the baseline

[1570] Risk and incidents New risks, near misses, escalations

[1573] Value realised Benefits claimed against benefits evidenced

[1576] Review or retire Re-authorise, improve, restrict or decommission

## Monitoring and human oversight are continuous duties held by the named owner, not a phase that ends at go-live. [1578]

## Where this guide sits [1579]

[1580] The hierarchy of AI-related guidance a public-sector team works inside. This guide is a proposal: it interprets and sequences the guidance above it, and it does not replace or override any of it.

## International frameworks [1582]

[1583] OECD AI Principles, EU AI Act risk tiers, ISO/IEC 42001 management standards.

## UK statute and cross-government policy [1585]

[1586] Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR, Equality Act 2010, Procurement Act 2023, the AI Opportunities Action Plan.

## Central guidance in force [1588]

[1589] AI Playbook for the UK Government, Service Standard, Technology Code of Practice, ATRS, Data Ethics Framework, NCSC secure-AI guidelines.

## Departmental policy and standards [1591]

[1592] Organisational AI policy, data classification, security standards, delegated authority and spend controls.

## This implementation guide [1595]

[1596] AI Capability Governance and Implementation — 69 chapters, assessment tools and register schemas that turn the guidance above into delivery.

[1598] Proposal

## Team-level artefacts [1600]

[1601] Agent register entries, ATRS records, assurance evidence, instruction blocks and cost models.

## Multidisciplinary from the outset [1607]

[1608] Every source in this app lands on the same point. The AI Playbook makes skills and expertise a principle in its own right. The Service Manual builds the multidisciplinary team into the Service Standard. NCSC wrote its secure-AI guidelines for data scientists, developers, managers, decision-makers and risk owners together. The roster is in Teams ; the readiness barometer is in the Observatory .

[1611] Back to the contents · Suggest a correction (opens GitHub)

[1623] Responsible AI · start here

## What do you want to do? [1624]

[1625] Start from your task. This part of the playbook routes you to the proportionate tool, template, assessment or support. Governance follows what the AI can see, create and do, not which company made it.

[1629] Quick route selector · five questions

## Can I use AI for this? [1630]

## 1. Would the output decide, or directly change, someone’s rights, entitlements, safety or access to a service? [1632]

## 2. Will you use personal data or information marked OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE or above? [1634]

## 3. Can the AI take actions, run on a schedule or work through several steps without you? [1636]

## 4. Is there an approved tool in your organisation's catalogue that already does this? [1638]

## 5. Could a conventional rule, form or automation do the job reliably? [1640]

[1642] Your route

## Answer the five questions [1643]

[1644] The route appears when every question has an answer. “Not sure” is a valid answer.

[1645] A first sort, not an approval. Any route other than an approved tool leads to a registered use case.

## Six things to know first [1646]

## AI concepts and limitations [1649]

[1650] Generative AI predicts plausible output. It can be fluent and wrong at once, so outputs need checking in proportion to what depends on them.

## Models and providers [1652]

[1653] A product can use several models from several providers, sometimes chosen automatically. The model can change without the product name changing.

## Enterprise grounding [1655]

[1656] Grounding feeds organisational content to the model. Whatever the index can reach, the AI can surface, including titles, filenames and metadata.

## Agents, tools and actions [1658]

[1659] An agent plans steps and uses tools to act: send, update, create or call other agents. Acting changes the risk boundary.

## Human oversight [1661]

[1662] Oversight works only if the reviewer has the competence, the evidence and the authority to challenge, override or stop.

## Deployment route [1664]

[1665] The same model reached directly, through a cloud platform or inside another supplier’s product is a different governance object each time.

## For everyone in the organisation [1666]

[1671] All colleagues Find guidance, approved tools and practical help

[1676] Leaders and managers Make informed decisions, manage risk and value

[1681] Risk, security and compliance Assure, monitor and advise

[1686] IT and digital Enable, integrate and manage

[1691] Data and information Ensure data is ready and well managed

[1696] Commercial and procurement Manage suppliers, licences and costs

[1701] Accessibility and inclusion Support all users and workplace adjustments

[1706] Policy, strategy and transformation Drive adoption, value and continuous improvement

## Enabled by common services [1708]

[1710] Real-world outcomes · turning responsible AI into a stronger public sector

## Safer services for citizens [1715]

## Greater value for taxpayers [1719]

## More efficient working [1723]

## More inclusive for all [1727]

## A more innovative public sector [1731]

## Ideas → responsible implementation → trusted operation → lasting public value [1732]

## Govern the capability and behaviour first [1734]

[1735] Microsoft Copilot, Anthropic Claude, GitHub Copilot, Gemini and future tools sit as product overlays beneath one common control model. Role routes for every audience are in How to use this guide.

## Get help [1738]

## Using an approved tool [1739]

[1740] Your IT service desk, then the product’s support route.

## Assessing a use case [1741]

[1742] The AI assurance team owns screening and the decision register.

## An incident or concern [1743]

[1744] Report through the incident route on the Operate page. Treat data exposure as a security incident.

## Accessibility or adjustments [1745]

[1746] Your line manager and workplace adjustments service.

[1747] Named contacts are set by each organisation when the guidance is deployed.

## Standards and policy [1749]

[1751] Your organisation’s AI policy and acceptable use.

## Government guidance [1752]

[1753] The AI Playbook for the UK Government.

## AI Playbook on GOV.UK ↗ [1754]

## Data protection [1755]

[1756] UK GDPR, DPIAs and international transfers.

[1759] Threat modelling, secure configuration and incident response.

## Records [1760]

[1786] Start here · orientation

## How to use this guide [1787]

[1788] 87 chapters in 12 parts. Nobody needs all of it. Pick a reading mode, then a route.

## Front to back [1794]

[1795] 12 parts in delivery order: decide, build, assure, operate, fund, the people and pilot material, then the deployment part and the reference. Roughly a day's read.

## By role route [1799]

[1800] 10 routes below, each an ordered set of chapters for one job. Twenty to forty minutes.

## By task [1804]

[1805] Use the launchpad or search: rate readiness, tier an agent, price a job, build an instruction block, check exit readiness.

## Routes by role [1806]

[1807] Each route is an ordered set of chapters. Click any step to jump there.

## Data and information [1809]

[1810] Get data ready, keep metadata and indexing honest, govern connectors and treat AI outputs as records.

## All colleagues [1812]

[1813] Find an approved tool, get a route for your task, and know where to get help.

## Accountable leader or SRO [1815]

[1816] Decide where AI is worth the risk and the spend, and be able to answer for it.

## Service owner [1818]

[1819] Adopt agents without destabilising a service people depend on.

## Product or delivery manager [1821]

[1822] Frame the problem, prove the value, keep the team moving.

## AI engineer or technical owner [1824]

[1825] Build well-grounded agents and prove they work.

## Assurance, ethics or audit [1827]

[1828] Apply proportionate control and see the evidence behind it.

## Commercial, finance or FinOps [1830]

[1831] Fund adoption honestly and keep exit possible.

## People, learning and adoption [1833]

[1834] Build capability that outlasts the pilot.

## Pilot participant [1836]

[1837] Use the guide during a real deployment and record what happens.

## What each part is for [1838]

## 1 · Start here [1841]

[1843] What the guidance says, what this guide adds, and the ten capability domains it all rests on.

## 2 · Decide and prioritise [1846]

[1848] Whether to do it at all: evidence quality, use-case selection, criticality and the assurance tier that follows.

## 3 · Design and build [1851]

[1853] Capability class — generative, agentic or declarative — then instructions, architecture, grounding and the autonomy boundary.

## 4 · Assure and govern [1856]

[1858] The trust cycle, the operating model, risks and mitigations, registers, transparency records and recovery.

## 5 · Operate and oversee [1861]

[1863] Life after approval: the portfolio view, the agent lifecycle, public-service impact and readiness tracking.

## 6 · Fund and buy [1866]

[1868] The full investment line, unit economics, supplier requirements and exit.

## 7 · People and adoption [1871]

[1873] Teams, roles, pathways, inclusion and the organisational adoption programme.

## 8 · Live pilot [1876]

[1878] How this guide is being tested in a real deployment, and what would justify a permanent toolkit.

## 9 · Product documentation [1881]

[1883] Requirements, architecture, design, theory of change and the research base for the guide itself.

## 10 · Knowledge and navigation [1886]

[1888] Glossary, thesaurus, generated knowledge graph, taxonomies, ontology, site map, guided tours and platform links.

## 11 · Deploy for real [1891]

[1893] The part that turns the guide into a deployment: fifty-four real services placed on volume and criticality, a generator that derives the whole governance set for any case, four agents carried end to end — one in each quadrant — and an explicit list of what this guide still does not cover.

## 12 · Reference [1896]

[1898] Devolved and international comparators, and every source behind the content.

## How to read the labels [1901]

[1902] Verified Present in a surfaced source.

[1905] Interpretation A conclusion drawn across sources.

[1908] Proposal Recommended future state, not adopted policy.

[1911] Illustrative Looks like data, carries no measured source.

## What this guide is not [1915]

[1919] It does not override departmental policy, professional advice or formal approvals.

[1923] It is not the register of record for any live deployment.

[1927] It holds no personal, case or OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE data; assessments stay on your device.

[1931] It cannot issue an approval — the accountable owner does that.

[1932] Back to the contents · Suggest a correction (opens GitHub)

[1944] The playbook

## Ten principles, one life cycle [1945]

[1946] The AI Playbook for the UK Government (opens an external website) (GDS, 10 February 2025) supersedes the Generative AI Framework and covers all AI: machine learning, NLP, computer vision, generative and agentic systems. The ten principles are paraphrased below; open each for its first moves.

## The deployment life cycle [1950]

[1951] Playbook principle 5: manage the whole life cycle, including the unglamorous parts. Each stage has a gate; nothing moves right without passing it.

[1954] Stage 1

## Discover [1955]

[1957] Frame the problem and the user need: is AI the right tool at all?

[1958] Triage risk: personal data, decisions about people, public-facing?

[1959] Assemble the multidisciplinary team; screen for DPIA and equality impacts

[1961] Gate · A named SRO and a written problem statement

[1964] Stage 2

## Design [1965]

[1967] Decide buy vs build; source and assess the data

[1968] Threat-model with security; place the human-oversight points

[1969] Legal, ethics and commercial shape the approach, not the finished thing

[1971] Gate · DPIA drafted; risks owned; oversight designed in

[1974] Stage 3

## Build & evaluate [1975]

[1977] Develop securely; verify the model and data supply chain

[1978] Evaluate accuracy, bias and robustness against agreed baselines

[1979] Red-team it: prompt injection, misuse, edge cases

[1981] Gate · Evaluation results reviewed by the whole team

[1984] Stage 4

## Deploy [1985]

[1987] Pass assurance gates; publish the ATRS record

[1988] Switch on human review and incident response

[1989] Tell users they are interacting with AI

[1991] Gate · Assurance sign-off; transparency record live

[1994] Stage 5

## Operate & retire [1995]

[1997] Monitor drift, bias and hallucination in production

[1998] Re-evaluate on every model or data update

[1999] Plan decommissioning and knowledge handover

[2001] Gate · Monitoring dashboards live; exit plan on file

[2003] Back to the contents · Suggest a correction (opens GitHub)

[2015] The domains

## Five lenses on every deployment [2016]

[2017] Cyber, data, digital, technology, and the legal-ethical frame around them. Each domain has its own authoritative guidance; a deployment is ready only when all five say so. That is why the team is multidisciplinary.

[2021] Cyber

## Cyber security [2022]

## NCSC secure AI guidelines [2023]

## NCSC machine learning principles [2026]

## Secure by Design (UK Government) [2029]

[2033] NCSC Guidelines for secure AI system development cover secure design, development, deployment and operation. Agreed with CISA and 21 international agencies; aimed at any system that uses AI, built or bought.

[2034] Secure by Design and the Government Cyber Security Standard apply to AI services like any other, plus AI-specific threat modelling: prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction, over-permissioned agents.

[2035] NCSC's principles for the security of machine learning translate the threats into controls. Walk before you run with agentic AI.

[2038] Data

## Data & information [2039]

## Data Ethics Framework [2040]

## ICO: AI and data protection [2043]

## ATRS hub [2046]

[2050] The Data Ethics Framework guides appropriate, responsible data use across the public sector: transparency, accountability, fairness.

[2051] UK GDPR and the DPA 2018 require a DPIA before high-risk processing. The ICO's AI guidance, with a statutory AI code of practice in development, is the regulator's view of what good looks like. Cross-border processing (for example a US-processed model behind a UK product) needs a Transfer Risk Assessment as well as SCCs.

[2052] The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard is mandatory for central departments and arms-length bodies: a published record for every in-scope algorithmic tool.

[2053] Model quality is data quality: govern provenance, representativeness and retention for training and grounding data alike — retrieval systems inherit the permissions, quality and currency of the estate.

[2056] Digital

## Digital & service [2057]

## Service Standard [2058]

## AI Playbook for the UK Government [2061]

## AI Knowledge Hub [2064]

[2068] The Service Standard and Service Manual set the operating model: start with user needs, work in multidisciplinary teams, iterate in the open. AI services are still services.

[2069] The AI Playbook and the AI Knowledge Hub supply the patterns, case studies and communities; the PM's AI Exemplars programme is the test-and-learn engine for scaling what works.

[2070] Accessibility is law, not polish: WCAG 2.2 AA under the Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018. AI interfaces (chat, voice, summaries) need their own accessibility evidence.

[2073] Technology

## Technology & architecture [2074]

## Technology Code of Practice [2075]

## AI Opportunities Action Plan [2078]

## Action Plan delivery progress [2081]

[2085] The Technology Code of Practice governs the technology choices: cloud first, interoperability, open standards, sustainability, exit.

[2086] Compute and infrastructure are national policy: AI Growth Zones and a compute roadmap from 21 ExaFLOPs (2025) towards 420 by 2030 under the AI Opportunities Action Plan.

[2087] Buy well: use Crown Commercial Service AI routes, insist on evaluation access and model-change notice in contracts, and design the exit before signing the entry.

[2090] Legal & ethics

## Legal, ethics & society [2091]

## Explaining decisions made with AI [2092]

## Data Ethics Framework [2095]

## Equality Act 2010 guidance [2098]

[2102] The Equality Act 2010 and the Public Sector Equality Duty apply to automated and AI-assisted decisions. Public-law duties (fairness, rationality, giving reasons) still bind when a model is in the loop.

[2103] Explainability has a manual: 'Explaining decisions made with AI', by the ICO and The Alan Turing Institute — and explanations shown to people should reference functional needs, never a diagnosis or label.

[2104] Public trust is earned in the open: engage affected people early, say clearly where AI is used, and give a route to challenge and redress.

[2105] Back to the contents · Suggest a correction (opens GitHub)

# Responsible use of AI assistive technology

[Open this section on the publisher’s website](https://cyberdudeuk.github.io/ai-capability-governance/#practice)

The numbers in brackets identify elements in the ordered DOM inventory. This is a text projection of Em’s material.

## Responsible use of AI assistive technology [19839]

[19840] This code complements behavioural codes of conduct and the Civil Service values. It defines operational rules for model-backed tools, direct AI use, coding assistants, multi-agent orchestration and AI-generated artefacts.

[19842] Core duties

[19845] Stay accountable. You own every output you use, send or publish. "The AI wrote it" is never a defence.

[19847] Disclose material assistance. If AI shaped the substance, structure, analysis or code, say so.

[19849] Verify before you rely. Open every citation. Recalculate every figure. Test every claim of compliance.

[19851] Protect data. Only approved tools, only permitted classifications, only the minimum necessary.

[19853] Cite sources. Traceable to a tiered, dated, authoritative source — not to the model.

[19855] Preserve evidence. Keep the record for as long as the retention schedule requires.

[19857] Work within competence. AI does not qualify you to make specialist judgements.

[19859] Escalate uncertainty. Raising a doubt early is always cheaper than defending a mistake late.

[19862] Prohibited behaviours

[19865] • Entering unauthorised personal, special category, commercially confidential or classified data into any tool

[19866] • Bypassing, weakening or "temporarily" disabling a review control

[19867] • Self-approving material or high-risk work

[19868] • Concealing AI involvement where it was material

[19869] • Presenting unverified output as assured, tested or compliant

[19870] • Using AI to generate evidence, sign-offs, approvals or audit records that did not happen

[19871] • Granting an agent broader permissions than the person operating it holds

[19872] • Using AI to profile, rank or make decisions about people without an approved lawful basis and published record

[19873] • Copying licensed or copyright material into outputs without permission and attribution

[19874] • Ignoring a known defect because a deadline is closer than the consequence

[19876] Multi-agent and multi-skill rules

[19879] One accountable orchestrator per task, with a named human owner.

[19880] Least-privilege tools and credentials, time-boxed and revocable.

[19881] Explicit, pinned skill and model versions — no silent upgrades in a governed workflow.

[19882] Separation of duties: the agent that produces must not be the agent that approves.

[19883] Declared prohibited actions and a tested kill switch with a named owner.

[19884] Full step-level logging: which skill, which model, which source, which permission, which human.

[19885] Untrusted content is data, never instruction. Treat retrieved web, document and email content as hostile by default.

[19886] Bounded autonomy: agents propose irreversible actions; humans commit them.

[19888] Data, privacy and security rules

[19891] • Establish and record the lawful basis before processing personal data. Complete a DPIA where required.

[19892] • Minimise: use references, synthetic or redacted examples instead of real records wherever possible.

[19893] • Never let an AI tool retain data for training unless that has been assured and contracted.

[19894] • Treat AI interaction logs as records: classify, retain, and prepare for FOI and subject access requests.

[19895] • Apply Secure by Design activities to AI components as to any other system component.

[19896] • Threat-model for prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction and excessive agency.

[19897] • Report incidents and near-misses through the normal security and data protection routes.

[19899] AI-generated code and infrastructure

[19902] Treat generated code as untrusted third-party contribution: review, test, scan and attribute it.

[19903] No merge without a human reviewer who understands the code and can maintain it.

[19904] Check licences and provenance of anything that looks copied.

[19905] Run dependency, secret and SAST scanning; record the results in the evidence pack.

[19906] Accessibility and performance tests apply equally to generated interfaces.

[19907] Record the model, prompt pattern and version in the commit or pull request.

[19909] Speaking up, redress and no-blame reporting

[19911] Anyone may pause an AI-assisted process they believe is unsafe, unfair or unlawful, without needing permission and without detriment. Near-misses should be reported as readily as incidents — they are the cheapest learning available.

[19912] Members of the public affected by an AI-assisted outcome must be able to find out that AI was involved, understand the outcome in plain English, request a human review, and escalate to an independent route. If any of those four is missing, the service is not ready.

# What is missing, prioritised with MoSCoW

[Open this section on the publisher’s website](https://cyberdudeuk.github.io/ai-capability-governance/#roadmap)

The numbers in brackets identify elements in the ordered DOM inventory. This is a text projection of Em’s material.

## What is missing, prioritised with MoSCoW [22074]

[22075] An honest backlog is a trust signal. These are the gaps identified in this portal and in most public sector AI guidance, ordered by whether they are essential, valuable, desirable or deliberately out of scope.

[22077] All

[22078] Must have

[22079] Should have

[22080] Could have

[22081] Won't have (this time)

## Named accountable owner and published contact route [22085]

[22086] Nothing on this page is credible without a person who owns it and answers questions.

## Accessibility statement, testing evidence and feedback route [22089]

[22090] Legally required for UK public sector sites; also the fastest trust signal.

## Version, last-reviewed and next-review dates on every artefact [22093]

[22094] Freshness is the main failure mode of guidance portals.

## Machine-readable metadata schema published openly [22097]

[22098] Without a schema, registries cannot federate and evidence cannot be automated.

## Risk-based human review model with no self-approval [22101]

[22102] The core control that keeps accountability with people.

## Source citation and provenance for every claim [22105]

[22106] Prevents hallucination becoming policy.

## DEIA screening built into the default workflow [22109]

[22110] Equality duty is a due-regard duty — it must happen before decisions, not after.

## Search across the whole corpus with filters and permalinks [22113]

[22114] Findability is the top usability complaint for guidance sites.

## Role-based entry points and task-first navigation [22117]

[22118] Users arrive with a task, not an interest in your information architecture.

## Downloadable, offline and printable formats [22121]

[22122] Supports assisted digital, low bandwidth and audit contexts.

## Worked examples and anti-patterns for each control [22125]

[22126] Abstract principles do not change behaviour; examples do.

## Change log and subscribe-to-updates [22129]

[22130] Lets teams re-check work when guidance changes.

## Multilingual and alternative-format provision (Welsh, Easy Read, BSL) [22133]

[22134] Statutory in some contexts and essential for inclusion in all.

## Automated link-health and freshness checking [22137]

[22138] Broken authority links silently destroy trust.

## API and JSON export of the registry and corpus [22141]

[22142] Enables reuse by other departments and tooling.

## Maturity self-assessment with benchmarking [22145]

[22146] Helps organisations see where they are without a consultant.

## Community contribution workflow with moderation [22149]

[22150] Scales the corpus beyond a single team.

## Interactive decision tree for tool selection [22153]

[22154] Reduces the "which tool may I use?" support burden.

## Carbon and cost telemetry per model call [22157]

[22158] Makes proportionality measurable rather than rhetorical.

## Automated approval of any high-risk output [22161]

[22162] Out of scope by design — approval stays human.

## Storing personal or official-sensitive data in this portal [22165]

[22166] The portal is public and stateless; sensitive records belong in assured systems.

## Vendor-specific lock-in to a single model provider [22169]

[22170] Conflicts with interoperability and exit obligations.

## Replacing professional assurance roles [22173]

[22174] The toolkit supports specialists; it does not substitute for them.

# What practitioners and regulators are saying

[Open this section on the publisher’s website](https://cyberdudeuk.github.io/ai-capability-governance/#signals)

The numbers in brackets identify elements in the ordered DOM inventory. This is a text projection of Em’s material.

## What practitioners and regulators are saying [20914]

[20915] 29 signals on governing AI agents and the data they use, gathered from public LinkedIn content and refreshed weekly. Each names its author, links to where it was found and says how far it has been checked. Inclusion is not endorsement.

[20917] Read with care. LinkedIn does not allow automated reading of posts, so every summary comes from search-indexed text and is paraphrased. 15 of 29 come from vendors, consultancies or law firms and are marked. Statistics without a primary source are flagged as unverified. Check the source before you quote anything. The register is open data: ai-data-governance-signals.json (scanned 2026-11-09, version 1.2.0).

## UK public sector data leaders on data in action for public services [20928]

[20929] Lee Stockwell , Databricks · 2026

[20931] Activity highlights George Bettsworth, Head of Data Science at the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, putting AI progress down to good governance, with the argument that governance should sit at the data layer rather than in each application. Also trails an Innovation 2026 panel with Sue Bateman (Defra CDO), Jacqui Leggetter (DWP) and Aimee Smith (Government Chief Data Officer).

[20932] Why it matters: Direct UK government voices on governing AI through the data estate; supports BOT's position that agent governance starts with data governance.

[20934] Caution: Vendor-hosted content; the FCDO view is relayed by the vendor, not quoted from FCDO.

[20936] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Trusted third-party AI assurance: from principles to implementation [20946]

[20947] Elizabeth Seger , Tony Blair Institute for Global Change · 2026 (about one month before scan)

[20949] Argues AI governance is shifting from principles to implementation and that governance capacity is what lets organisations adopt AI agents safely. Points to the UK Government's Trusted Third-Party AI Assurance Roadmap (September 2025), tied to commitment 29 of the AI Opportunities Action Plan.

[20950] Why it matters: Links BOT's assurance pages to a named UK policy instrument and commitment number.

[20952] Caution: Roadmap and commitment number should be checked against GOV.UK before citing in BOT's evidence base.

[20954] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Scaling the Responsible Adoption of Agentic AI (techUK report) [20963]

[20964] Usman Ikhlaq , techUK (author); now University of Bath Institute for Policy Research · 21 July 2026

[20966] Profile lists a techUK report he authored on moving agentic AI beyond pilots to responsible deployment at scale across the UK economy, including how oversight and accountability keep pace.

[20967] Why it matters: UK industry baseline for agent oversight; a comparator for BOT's agent governance playbook.

[20969] Caution: Report itself not read; summary is from the profile listing.

[20971] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## AI Security Institute and NCSC advice on agentic AI cyber risk [20981]

[20982] AI Security Institute (AISI) , UK Government · 2026

[20984] AISI's page links to NCSC guidance on managing the cyber risk of agentic AI and to its Alignment Red Team work. The page describes AISI as part of the Cabinet Office.

[20985] Why it matters: Authoritative UK security sources BOT should cite for agent permissions and runtime controls.

[20987] Caution: Departmental home is as stated on the LinkedIn page; confirm on aisi.gov.uk given recent machinery of government changes.

[20989] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Agent autonomy, accountability and control boundaries in financial services [21000]

[21001] Keith Vincent (speaker); hosted by Ashurst Perkins Coie , Government Legal Department, Treasury Legal Advisers · 7 October 2026

[21003] Event activity frames AI agents around autonomy, accountability and where control boundaries sit, and notes that customers' own agents bring new liquidity and fraud risks.

[21004] Why it matters: Government legal perspective on the same question BOT answers: what an agent may do without a human.

[21006] Caution: Event summary written by the host firm, not by the speaker.

[21008] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## FCA moving towards agentic supervision [21018]

[21019] Sophie Sheldon (quoted in Law360 UK); liked by Devina Shah , Simmons & Simmons · 2026

[21021] Activity reports the FCA's plan to become an agentic regulator, with a warning about over-reliance on a single model, platform or provider, and separately references new FCA guidance on AI in financial services.

[21022] Why it matters: A UK regulator itself adopting agents: a live case for BOT's concentration-risk and vendor-neutrality guidance.

[21024] Caution: Secondary report via Law360; check the FCA's own statement.

[21026] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Responsible AI governance: beyond the 'Department of No' [21036]

[21037] Yasmin Liverpool , Chief Data Office, National Highways · Undated (likely 2025)

[21039] LinkedIn article proposing shared accountability for AI governance (for example the CDO with the CSO) or a cross-executive AI steering group, citing the NAO finding that poor data quality is a barrier to AI in government and the Generative AI Framework for HM Government as a starting point.

[21040] Why it matters: A practising government CDO's operating-model view; maps onto BOT's roles and accountability pages.

[21042] Caution: Predates later UK guidance that replaced the Generative AI Framework; treat as historical context.

[21044] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Most organisations will adopt agents before they can govern them [21053]

[21054] Melvyn White , Agentic AI strategy, governance and management (independent, London) · Current profile

[21056] Profile thesis: the gap between agent adoption and the ability to govern agents is the core risk.

[21057] Why it matters: A crisp framing of the governance-debt problem BOT exists to close.

[21059] Caution: Opinion; no evidence attached in the indexed text.

[21061] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Data governance must scale with AI adoption [21070]

[21071] Jake Boudsocq , Department of Government Services (Victoria, Australia) · 2026 (about five months before scan)

[21073] Takeaways from the 2026 Melbourne Data Protection and Security Summit: data governance is the operating model that makes responsible AI possible at scale; uncatalogued legacy data compounds risk; Digital Transformation Agency model clauses are becoming a public sector baseline; AI governance is not set-and-forget.

[21074] Why it matters: Peer-government evidence for BOT's 'know your data before AI' gate and for catalogue-first sequencing.

[21076] Caution: Australian context; DTA clauses are not UK instruments.

[21078] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## 2026 AI governance priorities, including governing AI agents [21087]

[21088] Partnership on AI (reposted by Stephanie Ifayemi) , Partnership on AI · 2026 (about eight months before scan)

[21090] Sets out priorities led by governing AI agents with accountability, security and privacy, plus stronger documentation and public reporting across the AI value chain and shared international baselines. Also notes work on how public sector AI governance differs from private sector approaches.

[21091] Why it matters: Multi-stakeholder agenda that BOT's agent registry and transparency pages already address.

[21093] Caution: Agenda-setting piece; not guidance.

[21095] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## From governance decisions to enforceable authority at runtime [21105]

[21106] Patrick Upmann , AIGN Global · 2026

[21108] As agents move from generating information to taking actions across data, tools and systems, the question becomes how governance decisions are enforced at runtime. Situates this against ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act.

[21109] Why it matters: Matches BOT's 'the app is the leash' principle: permissions enforced by scope, not policy text.

[21111] Caution: Author markets a proprietary governance framework.

[21113] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Agent scanners and an agent registry built on agent-card metadata [21123]

[21124] Roberto Mandiola , Amazon Web Services (post about MuleSoft and Google Cloud) · 2026

[21126] Describes scanners that find AI agents and capture metadata on what each can do, its underlying model and its data access rights, mapped to the agent-to-agent protocol's agent card so organisations hold one registry of agents, including home-built agents and MCP servers.

[21127] Why it matters: Strongest metadata link in this scan: an agent register is a metadata problem, which ties BOT to the Metadata Exchange Model and DCAT work.

[21129] Caution: Vendor announcement relayed in another person's activity feed (indexed under Andrea Radojicic's profile).

[21131] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Governing AI agents as data consumers [21141]

[21142] Bigeye (and others in the feed) , Bigeye · 2026

[21144] Argues that governing agents that read enterprise data differs from human-era data governance because agents fail at different points in the pipeline; recommends knowing data quality signals and what data agents access before rollout. The feed also cites a Sinch survey of 2,527 senior decision-makers in which 74% had rolled back a live agent after a governance failure.

[21145] Why it matters: Useful framing for BOT's data-access controls; the rollback figure is a candidate indicator.

[21147] Caution: Survey figure is vendor-reported and unverified; do not use in BOT's evidence base until the Sinch source is read.

[21149] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Unsanctioned agents as governance debt [21159]

[21160] Subeer Sehgal , Grazitti Interactive · 2026

[21162] A playbook for governing agents: where risk concentrates, which controls hold and how to prove compliance as agent numbers grow. Warns that unvalidated feedback loops, where agents treat their own inferences as fact, are the real blind spot. The company feed claims 54% of organisations have between 1 and 100 unsanctioned agents.

[21163] Why it matters: Supports BOT's agent inventory and lineage controls.

[21165] Caution: The 54% figure has no stated source; treat as unverified.

[21167] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Context engines and a knowledge layer for agents [21176]

[21177] Robert Noyce , Shell · 2026

[21179] Agents need business context, semantic definitions, governance, memory and trusted data; a knowledge layer linking business definitions to data gives agents that context.

[21180] Why it matters: Endorses the glossary, ontology and knowledge-graph layer the govukOS build standard already requires.

[21182] Caution: Practitioner reflection after an event; no evidence attached.

[21184] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## AI-ready data goes beyond data quality [21193]

[21194] Joyce Goh , Salesforce (Informatica) · 2026

[21196] Data readiness affects AI economics, and governance must evolve as AI moves from generating insight to agents taking action, needing more visibility, accountability and control.

[21197] Why it matters: Corroborates S01 and S09 from the platform side.

[21199] Caution: Vendor promotional content.

[21201] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Agents stretch the old data quality problem [21210]

[21211] Herman Yu , Teeup Data Technology · 2026

[21213] Data governance and data quality issues are long-standing; the non-deterministic behaviour of LLMs and agents stretches them further, so enterprise architecture must join governance dimensions into one framework.

[21214] Why it matters: Supports treating agent governance as an extension of data governance, not a new silo.

[21216] Caution: Opinion.

[21218] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## EU AI Act in force but enforcement readiness uneven [21227]

[21228] Robert Gasparovic , HAVEL & PARTNERS, Slovak Republic · 2026

[21230] Notes the EU AI Act has applied since 2 August 2026 but Member States differ in enforcement readiness; Europe is also revisiting text-and-data-mining rules.

[21231] Why it matters: Cross-border context for BOT's regulatory crosswalk.

[21233] Caution: Applicability dates differ by obligation under the Act; check the specific article before citing.

[21235] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## China's July 2026 framework for governing AI agents [21245]

[21246] Pascal Jiang (post by Rimon PC) , Dacheng Law Offices / Rimon PC · July 2026

[21248] Three measures effective July 2026 move China from principles to operational governance, including AI ethics guidance, a framework for anthropomorphic AI services and a policy framework for governing AI agents.

[21249] Why it matters: One of the first national-level agent governance frameworks; a comparator for BOT.

[21251] Caution: Law-firm summary; the primary texts are not read.

[21253] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Institutional readiness for responsible AI in the public sector [21262]

[21263] Anthony Akpan , Tizee Consult; Institutional AI Governance newsletter · April and July 2026

[21265] An SSRN preprint (April 2026) on institutional readiness as a condition for responsible AI in the public sector, and a newsletter launched in July 2026 on institutional responsibility in AI governance.

[21266] Why it matters: Academic framing of readiness that maps onto BOT's maturity and adoption model.

[21268] Caution: Preprint, not peer reviewed; focus is developing countries.

[21270] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## Five AI governance platforms compared [21280]

[21281] Brad Martineau , LinkedIn article · Undated

[21283] Compares Credo AI, IBM watsonx.governance, Holistic AI, Fiddler AI and Atlan, noting that a data governance and metadata platform such as Atlan supplies the lineage regulators expect.

[21284] Why it matters: Market scan only; useful for BOT's tooling landscape, not for recommendations.

[21286] Caution: Listicle; possible commercial interest. BOT stays vendor-neutral.

[21288] Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: search-indexed text, post not opened

## AI Security Institute publishes its inaugural Frontier AI Trends Report [21297]

[21298] Tess Buckley , Post about the AI Security Institute (DSIT) · 18 December 2025 (derived from the post's activity ID)

[21300] Post announcing that the UK AI Security Institute, part of DSIT, published its first Frontier AI Trends Report.

[21301] Why it matters: A UK government evidence source on frontier AI capability and risk that BOT's assurance material can cite once read at source.

## Semantic layer for agents: AI drafts business definitions, people certify them, agents answer in SQL [21399]

[21400] NVIDIA , Auto Ontology (open source, Apache 2.0) · November 2026 (repository read on 13 November 2026)

[21402] An open-source service that drafts an ontology from database metadata: business terms mapped to columns, reviewed SQL expressions, and the joins between tables. People then test it with real questions and certify the names, descriptions and SQL. An agent answers questions by writing SQL from those definitions, checks the query against the database, and returns the answer with its SQL and the steps it took. It serves this context to other agents over MCP, and says when a question cannot be answered from the data.

[21403] Why it matters: It makes certification a separate human step from drafting, which is where this toolkit's H0 to H5 review levels apply: see the advanced guide's worked examples on certifying a definition and reviewing an agent's answer, and the evidence pack's field for the definitions an answer relied on.

[21419] Luís Rodrigues , Not stated on the post (the author's headline describes him as a CPTO; he writes the newsletter Build What Matters) · About 7 November 2026 (the post showed '1w' when read on 17 November; the date is decoded from its activity ID)

[21421] Frames AI governance as four layers: regulation (the EU AI Act, plus GDPR, sector rules, NIS2 and DORA), standards and frameworks (ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI RMF), roles (a named owner for every AI system) and controls. Argues that controls are where most organisations fall short, and lists them: risk-rate every system, give agents only the tools they need, train people in AI literacy, keep a human able to stop the system, keep an inventory, log everything, and test continuously. Suggests starting with an inventory of every AI tool in use.

[21422] Why it matters: The four questions map onto this toolkit: the law (Resources, tier 0), proof (evidence pack builder, TK-04), accountability (the accountable owner and H4 to H5 review) and production (agent registry, TK-03, and incident reporting, TK-12).
