## Pick the route that matches your job today [893]

[894] Task-first entry points, because people arrive with a decision to make — not an interest in our information architecture.

## How much do you already know? [895]

[896] Choose a level, then a route below. Every route and task is marked with its level.

[900] New to AI in public services, or using this site for the first time. No technical knowledge needed.

[901] Start with: The four principles and the 2-minute review triage

[905] Then: Glossary and FAQ , transparency

[911] Using, buying or approving AI in your work, and need to show it is governed.

[912] Start with: H0–H5 review model and the evidence pack

[916] Then: Transparency record , resources , signals

[923] Building, assuring, integrating or reusing this guidance, including in code.

[924] Start with: Toolkit and the metadata schema

[928] Then: Authority tiering , open data , the repository

## Routes by role [933]

## New or occasional contributor [937]

[938] "I don’t want to get this wrong."

[939] Plain-language guidance, safe defaults, confidence prompts, buddying and clear role limits.

[940] Take the 5-minute triage, then use the declaration generator.

[942] Journey: Human review triage → Evidence pack → Code of practice

## Experienced practitioner [949]

[950] "Give me the fast, correct route."

[951] Direct links to standards, patterns, conformance packs, test scripts and evidence automation.

[952] Jump to the toolkit and copy the metadata schema.

[954] Journey: Toolkit → Metadata schema → Tools

## Specialist reviewer [961]

[962] "Show me what to challenge."

[963] Source-linked evidence, issue triage, risk decisions and assurance history.

[964] Use the H-level table and reviewer checklist.

[966] Journey: Reviewer checklist → Authority tiering → Signals

## Accountable owner / SRO [973]

[974] "What am I signing?"

[975] Risk overview, approval gates, residual risk, maturity dashboard and public transparency records.

[976] Generate the transparency record and check the MoSCoW roadmap.

[978] Journey: H0–H5 review model → Transparency record → Roadmap

## Supplier or delivery partner [985]

[986] "What will I be assessed against?"

[987] Published expectations, evidence formats, accessibility and security obligations, exit terms.

[988] Filter resources by procurement and security.

[990] Journey: Resources (procurement, security) → Catalogue metadata → Assurance

## Member of the public [997]

[998] "How is AI being used on my case?"

[999] Plain-English explanation, published records, how to challenge a decision and get support.

[1000] Read the transparency and redress commitments.

[1002] Journey: Transparency → Glossary and FAQ → Contact

## Data or AI governance lead [1009]

[1010] "What is changing, and does my data estate let us govern agents?"

[1011] Weekly signals with sources, the agent registry pattern, catalogue metadata for AI assets and the review model.

[1012] Start with this week's signals.

[1014] Journey: Signals → Agent registry (TK-03) → AI asset metadata → Review model

## Common tasks [1020]

## Decide how much human review my output needs [1025]

[1026] Answer six questions and get an H0–H5 level, the reviewers required and the evidence to keep.

## Write an AI-use declaration and evidence pack [1030]

[1031] Generate a copy-ready record of sources consulted, checks made and who approved what.

## Screen a change for equality and accessibility impact [1035]

[1036] Flag protected characteristics, access needs, assisted digital and exclusion risks early.

## Draft a public transparency record [1040]

[1041] Produce an ATRS-shaped record describing the tool, its purpose, data, oversight and risks.

## Check quantum and cryptographic exposure [1045]

[1046] Score harvest-now-decrypt-later risk against NCSC migration milestones.

## Find the authoritative source for a rule [1050]

[1051] Search 69 tiered laws, standards, guidance documents and tools.

[1053] Not sure whether to use AI at all? Ask three questions first: is there a simpler non-AI way to meet the user need; can you explain the decision to the person it affects; and could you defend this use at a public inquiry? If any answer is no, stop and seek advice.

[18370] The first rule that matches wins. A first sort, not an approval: every route other than an approved tool leads to a registered use case.

[18372] Would the output decide, or directly change, someone’s rights, entitlements, safety or access to a service?

[18382] Route

[18386] Q1 is Yes

[18387] Seek advice before going further

[18391] Q5 is Yes

[18392] Try conventional automation first

[18394] A rule, form or workflow is usually safer, cheaper and more consistent. Use AI only where judgement over unstructured material is the task.

[18412] Check for reuse, then register

[22002] A guidance utility that cannot be questioned is not trustworthy. Here is how this one is governed, and how you hold it to account.

## Provenance of this content [22005]

[22006] Every substantive claim links to a tiered source. Where this portal expresses an opinion or a house rule rather than a legal requirement, it says so.

[22019] CC BY 4.0 (content) / MIT (code); Crown copyright material quoted here stays under the Open Government Licence v3.0. Fork it, adapt it for your organisation, and tell us what you changed so others benefit.

## Data and privacy [22021]

[22022] This site is static and client-side. It sets no tracking cookies, runs no analytics that identify you, and sends nothing you type in the tools to any server. Preferences are stored locally in your browser and you can clear them at any time.

## Known limitations [22024]

[22025] This is a concept portal, not a statutory instrument. It does not replace your organisation's policies, your DPO, your security team or your legal advice. Some linked standards sit behind paywalls.

## Report a problem [22027]

[22028] Tell us about a broken link, an out-of-date claim, an accessibility barrier or a gap. Accessibility issues get a response within five working days.

# Designed for real people, varied needs and accountable teams

[Open this section on the publisher’s website](https://cyberdudeuk.github.io/ai-capability-governance/#ucd)

The numbers in brackets identify elements in the ordered DOM inventory. This is a text projection of Em’s material.

## Designed for real people, varied needs and accountable teams [19761]

[19762] Inclusion is a delivery activity, not a compliance report. This section states what we commit to, how we test it, and how you can hold us to it.

## Design and research practice [19763]

## Start with user needs [19766]

[19767] Every asset traces to a named user need and a measurable outcome. If we cannot name the need, we do not build the feature.

[19768] Government Design Principles → (opens an external website)

## Research with the full range of users [19772]

[19773] Recruit disabled participants, assistive technology users, people with low digital confidence and people in vulnerable circumstances — in every round, not a one-off "accessibility round".

[19774] Inclusive research guidance → (opens an external website)

## Test with assistive technology [19778]

[19779] Manual testing with screen readers, magnification, voice control, switch access and keyboard-only. Automated tools catch a minority of real barriers.

[19780] ARIA Authoring Practices → (opens an external website)

## Design for the whole journey [19784]

[19785] Including offline, assisted digital, third-party support, and what happens when the AI is unavailable or wrong.

[19786] Assisted digital guidance → (opens an external website)

## Write for reading age 9 [19790]

[19791] Plain English, short sentences, no unexplained acronyms, inclusive terminology, and alternative formats on request.

[19792] Check your content →

## Measure exclusion, not just satisfaction [19795]

[19796] Track drop-out by channel and need, assisted digital volumes, complaint themes and accessibility issue ageing — and publish them.

[19797] Service Standard → (opens an external website)

## Accessibility commitments for this portal [19800]

## What we build in [19803]

[19805] Semantic HTML, landmarks and a logical heading order

[19806] Full keyboard operation with a visible, high-contrast focus indicator

[19807] Text contrast of at least 4.5:1 and 3:1 for interface components

[19808] Light, dark and high-contrast themes, plus a larger-text setting that persists

[19809] Respect for prefers-reduced-motion and no motion-only meaning

[19811] Responsive to 320 CSS px and to 400% zoom without loss of content

[19812] Status messages announced through ARIA live regions

[19813] No colour-only meaning; icons always paired with text

[19814] Descriptive link text that makes sense out of context

[19815] A print stylesheet that expands links and collapsible content

## How we test and report [19817]

[19819] Automated checks in the pipeline on every change

[19820] Manual keyboard and screen reader testing before release

[19821] Periodic testing with disabled participants

[19822] A published accessibility statement listing known gaps and fix dates

[19823] A named contact and a 5-working-day response commitment

[19824] Escalation route to the Equality Advisory and Support Service

[19825] Accessibility statement guidance → (opens an external website)

## DEIA in AI specifically [19828]

[19831] Known equity risks of AI-assisted delivery. Performance that degrades for under-represented groups; language models that default to majority dialects and names; outputs written above the reading age of the audience; automation that removes the human route people in crisis rely on; accessibility regressions in AI-generated code and content; and reviewers who trust fluent text more than accurate text.

[19834] What we do about them. Screen every change with the DEIA tool; disaggregate evaluation by affected group where lawful and proportionate; keep a human route that cannot be removed by efficiency targets; test AI-generated interfaces with assistive technology before merge; publish limitations honestly; and give people a real way to challenge an outcome.
